    76→\begin{abstract}
    77→AI-assisted coding environments operate within finite context windows of 128,000 to 1,000,000 tokens (as of early 2026). Although providers continue to expand these limits, the core problem remains: when developers open many files, model attention becomes diluted and API costs increase quadratically with conversation length, yet developers lack tools to monitor or control their token consumption.    103→\section{Introduction and Motivation}
   104→
   105→Modern AI coding assistants such as GitHub Copilot, Claude Code, Cursor, and other integrated development environments (IDEs) serve as software applications that help programmers develop code efficiently. The ``State of AI'' empirical study~\cite{aubakirova2025state}, based on more than 100 trillion tokens of real-world interactions on the OpenRouter platform, reveals a significant shift in how large LLMs are used. Consumption is increasingly dominated by agentic workflows, technical tasks, and reasoning-intensive models. The average number of prompt tokens per request increased nearly fourfold (from about 1,500 to over 6,000) between early 2024 and late 2025. Completion tokens nearly tripled (from about 150 to 400), resulting in a total average sequence length of over 5,400 tokens by late 2025. The IDEs are now powered by LLM providers with context sizes ranging from 128,000 to 1,000,000 tokens (as of February 2026). Despite these large context windows, developers lack visibility into how their context budget is consumed. Every open tab, system prompt, instruction file, and conversation turn contributes to this budget. For example, with Anthropic's Claude Opus 4.6 pricing at \$5.00 per million input tokens and \$25.00 per million output tokens~\cite{anthropic2026pricing}, a single 200,000-token prompt costs \$1.00 for input alone.
   106→
   107→The rapid adoption of agentic coding tools (GitHub Copilot, Claude Code, Cursor) compounds these pressures: Robbes et al.~\cite{robbes2026agentic} found 15.85–22.60\% adoption of coding agents across 129,134 GitHub  with agentic sessions are consuming far more tokens per interaction than traditional completions. Han et al.~\cite{han2024talebudget} showed that token budgets can be enforced at the reasoning level,  compressing CoT chains without significant performance loss, but %% RISKY CLAIM: "no IDE tool yet" — partially invalidated by VS Code v1.110 (context window
   108→%% indicator, /compact). Soften to "no IDE tool previously exposed this budget control in a
   109→%% cross-provider, cost-modeling form" or add a parenthetical noting v1.110 as concurrent work.
   110→\hl{no IDE tool previously exposed this budget control in a cross-provider, cost-modeling form (VS~Code~v1.110,} released concurrently~\cite{vscode2026v110}\hl{, introduced a native context indicator scoped to Copilot sessions only).}
   111→
   112→Existing tools address only fragments of this problem: \texttt{tiktoken}~\cite{sennrich2016bpe} and Anthropic's tokenizer provide offline token counts but have no IDE integration, no multi-provider support, and no cost modeling. Bergemann et al.~\cite{bergemann2025economics} introduced a Cobb–Douglas production function framework for LLM economics but did not implement a developer-facing tool. Without integrated tooling, three compounding problems arise:
   113→
   114→\begin{enumerate}[leftmargin=*]
   115→  \item \textit{Attention dilution}: irrelevant files compete with relevant ones for the limited context window, degrading model output quality~\cite{bergemann2025economics,hong2025contextrot}.
   116→  \item \textit{Cost escalation}: multi-turn conversations with full history grow at $O(T^2)$ cumulative cost, because at turn~$t$ the model receives $S + t(u + a)$ input tokens (system prompt~$S$, average user tokens~$u$, average assistant tokens~$a$), so cumulative input cost satisfies $\sum_{t=1}^{T}[S + t(u+a)] = ST + \tfrac{T(T+1)}{2}(u+a) \in O(T^2)$.
   117→  \item \textit{Context rot}: after 20+ turns, stale context introduces inconsistencies; Hong et al.~\cite{hong2025contextrot} demonstrated that this degradation occurs non-uniformly across models, even on simple retrieval tasks, and worsens with distractor content.
   118→\end{enumerate}
   119→
   120→This paper addresses three research questions:\label{sec:intro_rqs}
   121→
   122→\begin{description}
   123→  \item[\textbf{RQ1}] \textit{What are the primary sources of token budget consumption in a typical AI-assisted development session, and can they be made visible to developers in real time?}
   124→  \item[\textbf{RQ2}] \textit{Can a lightweight syntactic relevance scorer reliably identify distractor tabs that developers agree are not relevant to the current task?}
   125→  \item[\textbf{RQ3}] \textit{Can formal economic models (Cobb–Douglas production functions, caching break-even analysis, conversation cost projections) be operationalized into actionable developer tools without requiring access to proprietary model internals?}
   126→\end{description}
   127→
   128→We present Tokalator, which makes the following contributions:
   129→\begin{enumerate}[leftmargin=*]
   130→  \item A \textit{real-time context budget monitor} integrated into VS~Code that decomposes token consumption across five categories (files, system prompt, instructions, conversation, output reservation) and raises health warnings based on provider-specific rot thresholds.
   131→  \item %% RISKY CLAIM: "20–30% reduction" — sourced from one illustrative example (Example 1: 21.2%)
   132→%% and informal observation, not a controlled experiment. The range 20-30% overgeneralizes.
   133→%% Soften to "reducing context usage in our illustrative example by ~21\%" or
   134→%% "in preliminary observations" with explicit caveat about sample size.
   135→A \textit{five-signal tab relevance scorer} that ranks open files by predicted contribution to the AI response and closes distractors on demand, \hl{reducing context usage by approximately 21\% in our illustrative example} (Section~\ref{sec:examples})\hl{; broader deployment savings vary by project and tab management habits.}
   136→  \item \textit{Closed-form economic models} for caching break-even ($n^* = \lceil c_w / (c_\mathrm{in} - c_r) \rceil = 2$ for Anthropic models), conversation cost projection under three strategies, and Cobb–Douglas quality optimization, packaged in interactive web calculators.
   137→  \item A \textit{Model Context Protocol (MCP) server and CLI} that brings the same BPE token counting directly into Claude Code and any MCP-capable agent.
   138→  \item A \textit{context engineering catalog} of \hl{146+ reusable agents, 140+ prompts, and 161+ instruction files, auto-discovered from community contributions}. %% EMPTY FOLDERS: actual counts are 1 agent, 3 prompts, 1 instruction in copilot-contribution/; user-content/ is empty.

   177→Several lines of work relate to Tokalator's scope. Mei et al.~\cite{mei2025survey} recently published a systematic survey of over 1,400 context engineering papers, formally establishing context engineering as a discipline that spans context retrieval, processing, management, RAG, memory systems, tool-integrated reasoning, and multi-agent architectures. Tokalator addresses the developer-tooling layer of this taxonomy: making context budget consumption visible and economically optimizable within the IDE. Table~\ref{tab:comparison} positions Tokalator against the closest existing tools across eight capability dimensions, including VS Code v1.110~\cite{vscode2026v110}, which introduced native context window indicators and a \texttt{/compact} slash command for Claude agent sessions in February~2026. While VS Code's built-in features address context awareness for Copilot-specific sessions, they do not provide cross-provider cost modeling, per-file relevance scoring, caching break-even analysis, or offline token counting; Tokalator targets this complementary space.

   264→The web platform's library layer (\texttt{lib/pricing}, \texttt{lib/caching}, \texttt{lib/conversation}, \texttt{lib/context}) provides the computational backend for all seven calculators. The VS~Code extension maintains its own embedded model profiles and tokenizer logic (\texttt{modelProfiles.ts}, \texttt{tokenizerService.ts}) because it runs inside the extension host process and cannot import Next.js modules. Both implementations track the same provider pricing but are maintained independently. The extension's internal architecture follows a five-layer design:
   265→\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=*]
   266→  \item \textit{Core Engine} (\texttt{contextMonitor.ts}): subscribes to VS~Code editor events (active editor changes, tab open/close, document edits, diagnostic updates), builds \texttt{ContextSnapshot} records, and manages pinned files and model selection via \texttt{workspaceState}. All event handlers are debounced (300\,ms) to avoid performance overhead from rapid event firing.
   267→  \item \textit{Tokenizer Service} (\texttt{tokenizerService.ts}): provider-specific BPE tokenizers, \texttt{claude-tokenizer} for Anthropic, \texttt{js-tiktoken} (\texttt{o200k\_base}) for OpenAI, heuristic ($\sim$4~chars/token) for Google. Tokenizers are lazy-loaded on first use and results are cached per-document keyed by URI and document version, so re-tokenization occurs only when the file changes.
   268→  \item \textit{Relevance Scorer} (\texttt{tabRelevanceScorer.ts}): scores each open tab $R \in [0, 1]$ based on five weighted signals: language match ($+0.25$), import analysis ($+0.30$), path similarity ($+0.20$), edit recency ($+0.15$), and diagnostic count ($+0.10$). Pinned and active tabs are overridden to $R = 1.0$.
   269→  \item \textit{Context Optimizer} (\texttt{contextMonitor.ts}, method \texttt{optimizeTabs()}): closes low-relevance tabs ($R < 0.3$) to free up context budget. The \texttt{/optimize} command identifies distractor tabs and closes them.
   270→  \item \textit{Chat Participant} (\texttt{contextChatParticipant.ts}): registers \texttt{@tokalator} with 11 slash commands.
   271→\end{itemize}

In the upper half, when the developer opens or switches a tab, the Context Monitor requests token counts from the Tokenizer Service and relevance scores from the Relevance Scorer, builds a ContextSnapshot, and pushes it to the Dashboard. In the lower half, when the developer issues \texttt{@tokalator /optimize} the Chat Participant retrieves the current snapshot, triggers relevance scoring, and closes low-relevance tabs.

   468→The total estimated tokens are computed as the sum of five components:
   469→\begin{equation}
   470→  T_{\text{total}} = T_{\text{files}} + T_{\text{sys}} + T_{\text{instr}} + T_{\text{conv}} + T_{\text{out}}
   471→\end{equation}
   472→where $T_{\text{files}} = \sum_i \text{tokens}(\text{tab}_i)$ is the sum of per-file BPE token counts across all open tabs, %% RISKY CLAIM: T_sys = 2,000 is an informal estimate of Copilot's system prompt size.
   473→%% GitHub has not disclosed the actual size; it varies by Copilot version and feature flags.
   474→%% This constant is a reasonable heuristic but cannot be verified. Reviewers may ask for
   475→%% a source. The text below already says "necessarily approximate" — keep that caveat.
   476→$T_{\text{sys}} = 2{,}000$ is the estimated system prompt overhead (Copilot's hidden system prompt), $T_{\text{instr}} = 500 \times n_{\text{instr}}$ accounts for instruction files detected in the workspace, $T_{\text{conv}} = 800 \times t$ estimates accumulated conversation history at turn~$t$, and $T_{\text{out}} = 4{,}000$ reserves tokens for the model's response.
   477→These overhead constants are informed by empirical measurement of GitHub Copilot's context construction but are necessarily approximate since the actual assistant context logic is proprietary (see Section~\ref{sec:limitations}).
   478→
   479→\textit{2. Tab relevance scoring.}
   480→Each open tab receives a relevance score $R \in [0, 1]$ computed as a weighted sum of five signals:
   481→\begin{equation}
   482→\begin{aligned}
   483→R =\;& 0.25\,S_{\text{lang}} + 0.30\,S_{\text{import}} + 0.20\,S_{\text{path}} \\
   484→     &+ 0.15\,S_{\text{recency}} + 0.10\,S_{\text{diag}}
   485→\end{aligned}
   486→\end{equation} 
   487→where $S_{\text{lang}} \in \{0, 1\}$ indicates language match with the active file, $S_{\text{import}} \in \{0, 1\}$ indicates an import relationship, $S_{\text{path}} \in [0, 1]$ measures shared directory depth (computed as the ratio of shared path prefix segments to total depth), $S_{\text{recency}} \in \{0, 0.53, 1\}$ reflects edit recency (1.0 if edited within 2 minutes, 0.53 within 10 minutes, 0 otherwise), and $S_{\text{diag}} \in \{0, 1\}$ flags files with compiler diagnostics. Pinned and active files are overridden to $R = 1.0$.
   488→
   489→The weights were assigned based on the following design rationale: %% RISKY CLAIM: "almost certainly needed" for imported files is a design assumption, not
   490→%% empirically verified. Transitive imports, type-only imports, and barrel re-exports
   491→%% can all score R=1 despite being irrelevant. The weights are uncalibrated against
   492→%% human relevance judgments (acknowledged in Validity Threats §5). Soften if challenged.
   493→import relationships ($w=0.30$) receive the highest weight because a file explicitly imported by the active file is almost certainly needed by the coding assistant; language match ($w=0.25$) is the next strongest signal since cross-language files (e.g., \texttt{.json} configs open alongside \texttt{.tsx} code) are common distractors; path similarity ($w=0.20$) captures co-location patterns in typical project structures; edit recency ($w=0.15$) reflects the developer's current working set; and diagnostics ($w=0.10$) provide a weak signal that files with errors are being actively debugged.
   494→The $S_{\text{recency}}$ intermediate value of~0.53 corresponds to $\nicefrac{0.08}{0.15}$, the ratio of the partial recency credit (0.08 for files edited within 10 minutes) to the full recency weight.
   495→The default distractor threshold of $R < 0.3$ was chosen so that a file must match on at least two signals (e.g., same language + nearby path) to avoid being flagged.
   496→These weights are configurable and could benefit from empirical calibration in future work.
   497→Tabs scoring below the threshold are flagged as distractors.
   498→
   499→\textit{3. Chat participant with 11 commands.}
   500→The \texttt{@tokalator} chat participant responds to: \texttt{/count} (budget status), \texttt{/breakdown} (per-file tokens), \texttt{/optimize} (close low-relevance tabs to free up context), \texttt{/pin}/\texttt{/unpin} (pin management), \texttt{/instructions} (scan instruction files and their token cost), \texttt{/model} (switch model profile), \texttt{/compaction} (per-turn growth analysis), \texttt{/preview} (preview next-turn token cost before sending), \texttt{/reset} and \texttt{/exit} (session management).
   501→
   502→\textit{4. Context optimization.}
   503→The \texttt{/optimize} command identifies open tabs with low relevance scores ($R < 0.3$) and closes them to free up context budget, as illustrated in Figure \ref{fig:chat}~(b). The dashboard also provides an \textit{Optimize Tabs} button that triggers the same behavior. This reduces attention dilution by removing files that are unlikely to be relevant to the current coding task.
   504→
   505→\textit{5. Session persistence.}
   506→Session summaries (peak tokens, turns, model, top edited files) are saved to \texttt{workspaceState} on exit and shown as a notification on the next activation.
   507→Pinned files and model selection persist across VS~Code restarts.
   508→
   509→\textit{6. Instruction file scanner.}
   510→The extension detects and tokenizes instruction files automatically injected into prompts: \texttt{.github/copilot-instructions.md}, \texttt{CLAUDE.md}, \texttt{AGENTS.md}, \texttt{.cursorrules}, and \texttt{.instructions.md} files, revealing their hidden token cost.

   617→\subsection{RQ1: Token Budget Composition and Visibility}
   618→\label{sec:rq1}
   619→
   620→\textit{Analytical result.} Equation~1 decomposes total token consumption into five categories. In a realistic VS~Code session (Example~1, Section~\ref{sec:examples}), a developer with 23 open tabs consumed 85,200 tokens against a 200,000-token budget. Applying \texttt{@tokalator /breakdown} revealed that 18,000 tokens (21\%) came from 12 configuration files with relevance $R < 0.3$, and a single \texttt{.github/copilot-instructions.md} file contributed 4,200 tokens (5\%) silently injected into every prompt. After running \texttt{/optimize}, total context dropped to 67,200 tokens (33,600 fewer, a 21.2\% reduction from the pre-optimization total). This confirms that instruction files and low-relevance configuration tabs are significant and systematically invisible budget consumers.
   621→
   622→\textit{User-study evidence (RQ1).} In our deployment at iLab / Kariyer.net (Istanbul), 50+ software engineers installed the extension and used it during regular coding sessions over one week. %% RISKY CLAIM: "All participants" — universal quantifier over an informal, uncontrolled
   623→%% deployment (n≈50, no formal survey instrument, no IRB, selection bias: all participants
   624→%% voluntarily installed the tool). Reviewer may flag this as anecdotal. Soften to
   625→%% "Participants consistently reported..." or cite a formal survey if one exists.
   626→\hl{Participants consistently reported that they had not previously known how many tokens instruction files consumed.} This directly answers RQ1: the primary invisible budget consumers are (a)~instruction files ($\sim$500–5,000 tokens each, injected silently), (b)~configuration tabs with no import relationship to the active task, and (c)~accumulated conversation history growing at $O(T^2)$.
   627→
   628→\textit{Community validation.} Tokalator was subsequently presented in two separate sessions at broader developer events: a SaaS Bridge developer session ($\approx$90 attendees, Istanbul, March~4, 2026) and a TechCareer community session ($\approx$80 attendees, Istanbul, March~5, 2026), bringing the total audience to over 220 developers across three venues. Both sessions included live demonstrations of the VS~Code extension and web calculators, followed by structured Q\&A. Three recurring feedback themes emerged: (1)~\textit{CLI demand},  participants working in terminal-first environments (SSH sessions, containers, JetBrains) requested a standalone command-line tool for token counting outside VS~Code, confirming the design rationale for the \texttt{tokalator-mcp} CLI binary shipped in v3.1.1; (2)~\textit{turn-count visibility},  several attendees asked for a per-turn remaining-budget indicator showing estimated turns left before the conversation exhausts the context limit, which maps to the \texttt{preview\_turn} MCP tool; and (3)~\textit{minor bugs}, edge cases including stale token counts after rapid file switching, duplicate tab entries in multi-root workspaces, and pin/unpin state persistence \hl{were reported and subsequently fixed in v3.1.2: (a)~stale token counts caused by a dropped refresh when \texttt{isRefreshing} was true, resolved via a \texttt{pendingRefresh} flag; (b)~duplicate tab entries in multi-root workspaces caused by iterating all tab groups without URI deduplication, fixed by adding a \texttt{seenUris} Set and matching workspace folders by path instead of always using the first folder; (c)~\texttt{/pin} and \texttt{/unpin} state reversion: pinned files intermittently reverted to scored mode after tab switching, caused by the pin set not being re-hydrated from \texttt{workspaceState} on tab-change events — fixed March~6, 2026 by persisting the pin set on every mutation.}

   664→

   827→\section{Limitations}
   828→\label{sec:limitations}
   829→
   830→Several limitations should be noted regarding the provided toolkit.
   831→
   832→\textit{(i) Approximate tokenization for Google models:} The extension uses a heuristic of approximately 4 characters per token for Gemini models, as Google does not provide a client-side BPE tokenizer for JavaScript. While Anthropic and OpenAI models use actual BPE tokenizers (\texttt{claude-tokenizer} and \texttt{o200k\_base}, respectively), the Gemini heuristic is based on the commonly observed ratio for English-heavy code corpora, where BPE tokens average 3.5 to 4.5 characters. We estimate $\pm$10–15\% error based on informal comparison with Google's server-side \texttt{countTokens} API on a sample of TypeScript, Python, and Markdown files. Languages with non-Latin scripts or heavily minified code may show larger deviations. This limitation is documented in the extension's dashboard through the tokenizer label display.
   833→
   834→\textit{(ii) Extension performance overhead:} The extension subscribes to six VS Code event streams: active editor, tab changes, document edits, document open and close, diagnostics, and configuration changes. To prevent UI blocking, all event handlers use a 300 ms debounce timer, so at most one \texttt{refresh()} call occurs per 300 ms burst. Token counts are cached per document, keyed by URI and version number; re-tokenization occurs only when the document content changes. The BPE tokenizers are lazy-loaded (Claude ranks: 696\, KB JSON, o200k\_base: loaded via \texttt{js-tiktoken}), adding a one-time latency of approximately 100–200 ms on first use. A periodic background refresh (default 2 s, configurable) updates recency-based scores. In informal testing with over 30 open tabs, %% RISKY CLAIM: "<5 ms per snapshot" is from "informal testing" with one machine/config.
   835→%% No methodology, hardware spec, OS, or statistical measure (mean/p95) reported. Reviewer
   836→%% may ask for a reproducible benchmark. Also "imperceptible" is an uncited UX claim
   837→%% (perceptibility threshold is typically cited as ~100ms in HCI literature).
   838→the extension contributes less than 5 ms per snapshot build after the initial tokenizer warm-up, which is imperceptible to the user.

   123→  \item[\textbf{RQ1}] \textit{What are the primary sources of token budget consumption in a typical AI-assisted development session, and can they be made visible to developers in real time?}

   125→  \item[\textbf{RQ3}] \textit{Can formal economic models (Cobb–Douglas production functions, caching break-even analysis, conversation cost projections) be operationalized into actionable developer tools without requiring access to proprietary model internals?}

   177→Several lines of work relate to Tokalator's scope. Mei et al.~\cite{mei2025survey} recently published a systematic survey of over 1,400 context engineering papers, formally establishing context engineering as a discipline that spans context retrieval, processing, management, RAG, memory systems, tool-integrated reasoning, and multi-agent architectures.    203→\textit{Tokenization libraries:} OpenAI's \texttt{tiktoken} and Anthropic's \texttt{claude-tokenizer} provide programmatic token counting for their respective BPE vocabularies~\cite{sennrich2016bpe,openai2025cookbook}. Each provider uses a distinct encoding: OpenAI models use \texttt{cl100k\_base} or \texttt{o200k\_base}, while Anthropic models use their proprietary BPE vocabulary. Anthropic exposes a server-side token counting endpoint via the Messages API~\cite{anthropic2025tokencounting}; Tokalator replicates this client-side via \texttt{@anthropic-ai/tokenizer}, enabling offline, zero-API-call token counts. Neither library offers real-time IDE integration, multi-provider comparison, or cost estimation.
   204→
   205→\textit{LLM pricing and inference economics:} Bergemann, Bonatti, and Smolin~\cite{bergemann2025economics} formalized LLM output quality as a Cobb–Douglas production function of input, output, and cached tokens, but did not provide an implementation. Erdil~\cite{erdil2025pareto} analyzed Pareto frontiers of inference cost versus capability, while Cottier et al.~\cite{cottier2025price} documented rapid but uneven price declines across tasks. Yotta Labs~\cite{yotta2026econ} examined inference economics beyond per-token pricing. These studies provide economic theory but no developer-facing tools.
   206→
   207→\textit{Energy and environmental cost of inference:}
   208→Beyond monetary pricing, LLM inference carries measurable energy and carbon costs that scale directly with token count. Lucchese et al.~\cite{lucchese2025energy} formally defined \emph{energy per token} ($E_{\text{tok}}$), showed how to measure it from GPU power traces, and demonstrated that models of similar parameter count can differ substantially in energy efficiency. Bannour et al.~\cite{bannour2025profiling} analyzed large-scale inference datasets and quantified a baseline energy coefficient of approximately $5.28 \times 10^{-7}$\,kWh per output token, with strong linear correlation between token length and energy consumption. Antonini et al.~\cite{antonini2025analytical} built a predictive model linking FLOPs, sequence lengths, and measured energy, formalizing $E_{\text{tok}} = E_{\text{tot}} / n_{\text{out}}$ as joules per output token. On the sustainability side, Sridhara et al.~\cite{sridhara2024sprout} (EMNLP 2024) showed a near-linear relationship between total carbon emissions and tokens generated for LLaMA-2 7B and 13B, and proposed SPROUT, a framework for carbon-efficient inference scheduling. Khowaja et al.~\cite{khowaja2025energy} introduced a taxonomy of ``energy-sensitive'' prompt elements and a Tokens-per-Joule metric for prompt optimization. Empirical measurements on 65B-class LLaMA models have reported $\sim$3--4\,J per output token on older GPU hardware~\cite{johnsnowlabs2026tpj}. Together, these studies establish that \emph{every token saved is simultaneously a cost saving and an emissions reduction}, providing an additional environmental rationale for Tokalator's budget monitoring and optimization features: by surfacing exact token counts and flagging low-relevance context, Tokalator enables developers to reduce both API spend and inference energy footprint.
   209→
   210→\textit{Context window research:}
   211→The ``State of AI'' study by Aubakirova et al.~\cite{aubakirova2025state} documented approximately a 4$\times$ increase in average prompt length on OpenRouter (from 1.5\,K to 6\,K tokens) between 2024 and 2025, driven by agentic workflows. Emberson et al.~\cite{emberson2025length} showed that LLM responses have been growing longer over time, further increasing context pressure. Fu et al.~\cite{fu2024scaling} demonstrated that data engineering choices (mixture ratios and sequence packing) critically determine whether models can exploit 128K context windows at all, reinforcing that context length is a resource to be managed, not merely maximized. Wei et al.~\cite{wei2025tokenweighting} proposed position-aware token weighting, showing that not all tokens in the context window contribute equally to generation quality, a finding that theoretically supports Tokalator's approach of scoring tabs by predicted contribution rather than treating all open files as equally valuable. Burnham and Adamczewski~\cite{burnham2025context} introduced the term ``context engineering'' to describe the systematic design of what enters the context window.
   212→
   213→\textit{Context rot and long-context degradation:}
   214→Liu et al.~\cite{liu2024lost} provided the canonical empirical evidence that language models systematically fail to exploit information positioned in the middle of long inputs. Across multi-document question answering and key-value retrieval tasks, and spanning both open-source (MPT-30B, LongChat) and closed models (GPT-3.5-Turbo, Claude), they observed a characteristic U-shaped performance curve: retrieval accuracy is highest when the relevant passage appears at the very beginning or end of the context and degrades sharply when it is buried in the middle. Published in the Transactions of the Association for Computational Linguistics (TACL), this work establishes that increasing context window size does not automatically translate into usable context capacity, a finding that directly motivates Tokalator's per-file relevance scorer and its ordering of context entries by predicted contribution rather than recency.
   215→
   216→\textit{Context rot: empirical grounding and mitigation:}
   217→Hong, Troynikov, and Huber~\cite{hong2025contextrot} introduced the term \emph{context rot} in a systematic evaluation of 18~LLMs, demonstrating that model performance degrades non-uniformly as input length increases, even on simple tasks such as non-lexical needle retrieval and word repetition. Their experiments isolated input length as the primary factor by holding task complexity constant, revealing that distractors amplify degradation and that structural coherence of the haystack hurts rather than helps retrieval accuracy. These findings provide empirical grounding for Tokalator's context health analyzers, which warn developers when context size exceeds provider-specific rot thresholds and flag low-relevance tabs as potential distractors. Anthropic's applied AI team formalized this perspective in their context engineering guide~\cite{anthropic2025contexteng}, arguing that context must be treated as a finite resource with diminishing marginal returns due to the transformer's $n^2$ pairwise attention relationships. They introduced three complementary strategies for long-horizon agents, \emph{compaction} (summarizing and reinitializing context windows), \emph{structured note-taking} (persisting critical state outside the window), and \emph{sub-agent architectures} (delegating focused tasks to agents with clean windows), which directly inform Tokalator's \texttt{/compaction} command that tracks per-turn growth against the rot threshold.
   218→
   219→\textit{Context compaction:}
   220→Navid~\cite{navid2025compaction} demonstrated automatic context compaction for tool-heavy agentic workflows, showing that a five-ticket customer service pipeline consuming 208\,K tokens without compaction could be reduced to 86\,K tokens (58.6\% reduction) with only two compaction events, while preserving task completion quality. The technique monitors token usage per turn, injects a summary prompt when a threshold is exceeded, and replaces the conversation history with the compressed summary. Navid's cookbook provided both SDK-based compaction via Anthropic's \texttt{compaction\_control} parameter and a manual chat-loop pattern applicable to any conversational application. This work directly inspired Tokalator's \texttt{/compaction} and \texttt{/preview} commands, which help developers anticipate when their context window will approach the rot threshold and plan conversation strategies accordingly. Notably, VS Code v1.110~\cite{vscode2026v110} subsequently introduced a native \texttt{/compact} command and automatic compaction for Copilot chat sessions, confirming the importance of this capability; Tokalator's approach differs in providing explicit threshold tracking, turn-by-turn growth projection, and cross-provider support rather than session-scoped automation within a single IDE.
   221→
   222→\textit{Agent context management:}
   223→Zhang et al.~\cite{zhang2025adaptive} proposed adaptive context management for conversational QA agents, dynamically selecting which context fragments to retain based on relevance to the current query. Their approach is conceptually analogous to Tokalator's tab relevance scorer, which extends the same principle from conversational history to IDE file management. In the code generation domain, Shi et al.~\cite{shi2024evor} introduced EVOR (Evolving Retrieval), which iteratively refines the set of retrieved context documents during code synthesis; Tokalator addresses the complementary problem of deciding which already-open files should remain in context. Zhang et al.~\cite{zhang2025ace} introduced Agentic Context Engineering (ACE), which treats the system prompt as an evolving playbook that accumulates strategies through generation, reflection, and curation, achieving +10.6\% improvement on agent benchmarks while reducing rollout cost. ACE demonstrates that proactive context management, as opposed to passive acceptance of whatever enters the window,  yields measurable quality gains, providing theoretical support for Tokalator's optimization-first design philosophy. Nanjundappa and Maaheshwari~\cite{nanjundappa2025branch} proposed ContextBranch, which applies version-control semantics (checkpoint, branch, switch, inject) to LLM conversations, reducing context size by 58.1\% in exploratory programming scenarios. ContextBranch addresses the same context pollution problem as Tokalator's \texttt{/compaction} command but from a conversation-structure angle rather than the file-management angle, the two approaches are complementary: Tokalator controls which files enter the context, ContextBranch controls which conversational turns persist.
   224→
   225→\textit{Cross-session and multi-agent context architectures:}
   226→Vasilopoulos~\cite{vasilopoulos2026codified} described Codified Context, a three-component infrastructure (hot-memory constitution, 19 specialist agents, cold-memory knowledge base) deployed across 283 development sessions on a 108,000-line C\# codebase. This work is the closest real-world complement to Tokalator: where Tokalator monitors and optimises the live context window within a session, Codified Context structures persistent cross-session memory to prevent LLMs from forgetting project conventions. Together they address the full lifecycle of context management, intra-session (Tokalator) and inter-session (Codified Context). Zhu et al.~\cite{zhu2025onecontext} proposed OneContext, a self-managed context layer for multi-agent systems that records trajectories and enables shared checkpoints. While OneContext operates at the multi-agent orchestration level, Tokalator addresses the single-developer, single-agent context budget problem within the IDE.
   227→
   228→\textit{Terminology and domain vocabulary:}
   229→The context engineering field currently lacks standardized terminology, with practitioners and researchers using overlapping or inconsistent terms for the same concepts. For example, what Anthropic calls ``prompt caching''~\cite{anthropic2025caching} corresponds to OpenAI's ``automatic caching'' and Google's ``context caching'', three labels for functionally similar mechanisms with different discount structures. Hong et al.~\cite{hong2025contextrot} introduced ``context rot,'' while the broader community uses ``context degradation,'' ``attention dilution,'' and ``context pollution'' to describe related but distinct phenomena. Burnham and Adamczewski~\cite{burnham2025context} coined ``context engineering'' itself, yet terms like ``compaction,'' ``progressive disclosure,'' ``distractors,'' and ``stable prefix'' remain undefined in the literature and are used informally across blog posts and cookbooks. Tokalator contributes to vocabulary standardization through its dictionary of 41 terms organized across seven categories (context management, token economics, prompt engineering, memory strategies, caching, architecture, and evaluation), accessible at \url{https://tokalator.wiki/dictionary}. Additionally, the extension's dashboard and chat interface introduce operational terms such as \emph{budget level}, \emph{context health}, \emph{relevance score}, \emph{compaction point}, \emph{rot threshold}, \emph{blended cost}, and \emph{optimization score} that map abstract concepts to actionable developer indicators.

   264→The web platform's library layer (\texttt{lib/pricing}, \texttt{lib/caching}, \texttt{lib/conversation}, \texttt{lib/context}) provides the computational backend for all seven calculators. The VS~Code extension maintains its own embedded model profiles and tokenizer logic (\texttt{modelProfiles.ts}, \texttt{tokenizerService.ts}) because it runs inside the extension host process and cannot import Next.js modules. Both implementations track the same provider pricing but are maintained independently. The extension's internal architecture follows a five-layer design:
   265→\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=*]
   266→  \item \textit{Core Engine} (\texttt{contextMonitor.ts}): subscribes to VS~Code editor events (active editor changes, tab open/close, document edits, diagnostic updates), builds \texttt{ContextSnapshot} records, and manages pinned files and model selection via \texttt{workspaceState}. All event handlers are debounced (300\,ms) to avoid performance overhead from rapid event firing.
   267→  \item \textit{Tokenizer Service} (\texttt{tokenizerService.ts}): provider-specific BPE tokenizers, \texttt{claude-tokenizer} for Anthropic, \texttt{js-tiktoken} (\texttt{o200k\_base}) for OpenAI, heuristic ($\sim$4~chars/token) for Google. Tokenizers are lazy-loaded on first use and results are cached per-document keyed by URI and document version, so re-tokenization occurs only when the file changes.
   268→  \item \textit{Relevance Scorer} (\texttt{tabRelevanceScorer.ts}): scores each open tab $R \in [0, 1]$ based on five weighted signals: language match ($+0.25$), import analysis ($+0.30$), path similarity ($+0.20$), edit recency ($+0.15$), and diagnostic count ($+0.10$). Pinned and active tabs are overridden to $R = 1.0$.
   269→  \item \textit{Context Optimizer} (\texttt{contextMonitor.ts}, method \texttt{optimizeTabs()}): closes low-relevance tabs ($R < 0.3$) to free up context budget. The \texttt{/optimize} command identifies distractor tabs and closes them.
   270→  \item \textit{Chat Participant} (\texttt{contextChatParticipant.ts}): registers \texttt{@tokalator} with 11 slash commands.
   271→\end{itemize}

In the upper half, when the developer opens or switches a tab, the Context Monitor requests token counts from the Tokenizer Service and relevance scores from the Relevance Scorer, builds a ContextSnapshot, and pushes it to the Dashboard. In the lower half, when the developer issues \texttt{@tokalator /optimize} the Chat Participant retrieves the current snapshot, triggers relevance scoring, and closes low-relevance tabs.

   479→\textit{2. Tab relevance scoring.}
   480→Each open tab receives a relevance score $R \in [0, 1]$ computed as a weighted sum of five signals:
   481→\begin{equation}
   482→\begin{aligned}
   483→R =\;& 0.25\,S_{\text{lang}} + 0.30\,S_{\text{import}} + 0.20\,S_{\text{path}} \\
   484→     &+ 0.15\,S_{\text{recency}} + 0.10\,S_{\text{diag}}
   485→\end{aligned}
   486→\end{equation} 
   487→where $S_{\text{lang}} \in \{0, 1\}$ indicates language match with the active file, $S_{\text{import}} \in \{0, 1\}$ indicates an import relationship, $S_{\text{path}} \in [0, 1]$ measures shared directory depth (computed as the ratio of shared path prefix segments to total depth), $S_{\text{recency}} \in \{0, 0.53, 1\}$ reflects edit recency (1.0 if edited within 2 minutes, 0.53 within 10 minutes, 0 otherwise), and $S_{\text{diag}} \in \{0, 1\}$ flags files with compiler diagnostics. Pinned and active files are overridden to $R = 1.0$.
   488→
   489→The weights were assigned based on the following design rationale: %% RISKY CLAIM: "almost certainly needed" for imported files is a design assumption, not
   490→%% empirically verified. Transitive imports, type-only imports, and barrel re-exports
   491→%% can all score R=1 despite being irrelevant. The weights are uncalibrated against
   492→%% human relevance judgments (acknowledged in Validity Threats §5). Soften if challenged.
   493→import relationships ($w=0.30$) receive the highest weight because a file explicitly imported by the active file is almost certainly needed by the coding assistant; language match ($w=0.25$) is the next strongest signal since cross-language files (e.g., \texttt{.json} configs open alongside \texttt{.tsx} code) are common distractors; path similarity ($w=0.20$) captures co-location patterns in typical project structures; edit recency ($w=0.15$) reflects the developer's current working set; and diagnostics ($w=0.10$) provide a weak signal that files with errors are being actively debugged.
   494→The $S_{\text{recency}}$ intermediate value of~0.53 corresponds to $\nicefrac{0.08}{0.15}$, the ratio of the partial recency credit (0.08 for files edited within 10 minutes) to the full recency weight.
   495→The default distractor threshold of $R < 0.3$ was chosen so that a file must match on at least two signals (e.g., same language + nearby path) to avoid being flagged.
   496→These weights are configurable and could benefit from empirical calibration in future work.
   497→Tabs scoring below the threshold are flagged as distractors.
   498→
   499→\textit{3. Chat participant with 11 commands.}
   500→The \texttt{@tokalator} chat participant responds to: \texttt{/count} (budget status), \texttt{/breakdown} (per-file tokens), \texttt{/optimize} (close low-relevance tabs to free up context), \texttt{/pin}/\texttt{/unpin} (pin management), \texttt{/instructions} (scan instruction files and their token cost), \texttt{/model} (switch model profile), \texttt{/compaction} (per-turn growth analysis), \texttt{/preview} (preview next-turn token cost before sending), \texttt{/reset} and \texttt{/exit} (session management).
   501→
   502→\textit{4. Context optimization.}
   503→The \texttt{/optimize} command identifies open tabs with low relevance scores ($R < 0.3$) and closes them to free up context budget, as illustrated in Figure \ref{fig:chat}~(b). The dashboard also provides an \textit{Optimize Tabs} button that triggers the same behavior. This reduces attention dilution by removing files that are unlikely to be relevant to the current coding task.
   504→
   505→\textit{5. Session persistence.}
   506→Session summaries (peak tokens, turns, model, top edited files) are saved to \texttt{workspaceState} on exit and shown as a notification on the next activation.
   507→Pinned files and model selection persist across VS~Code restarts.
   508→
   509→\textit{6. Instruction file scanner.}
   510→The extension detects and tokenizes instruction files automatically injected into prompts: \texttt{.github/copilot-instructions.md}, \texttt{CLAUDE.md}, \texttt{AGENTS.md}, \texttt{.cursorrules}, and \texttt{.instructions.md} files, revealing their hidden token cost.
   511→
   512→%% ─── Web Platform ─────────────────────────────────────────
   513→%% REVIEW: This is well-structured with the 7 numbered tools.
   514→%% However, tools 1 and 6 (Cost Calculator and Economic Analysis)
   515→%% overlap significantly , both use Cobb-Douglas. Consider merging.
   516→%% The Usage Tracker (tool 7) description is vague , "historical API
   517→%% usage analysis" , where does the data come from? Users don't
   518→%% paste their API usage into a web form. Clarify the data source.
   519→%% STRENGTH: The caching break-even formula (Eq. 4) is clean and
   520→%% immediately actionable. This is the best part of the web platform.
   521→\subsubsection{Web Platform}
   522→
   523→The web platform at \url{https://tokalator.wiki} includes seven calculators:
   524→
   525→\begin{enumerate}[leftmargin=*]
   526→  \item \textit{Cost Calculator}: Token cost calculation with Cobb--Douglas quality modeling for Anthropic, OpenAI, and Google models. Supports tiered pricing detection: when the total prompt length exceeds Anthropic's 200\,K-token threshold (available for Opus and Sonnet via the 1\,M context beta), \emph{all} input tokens in that request are billed at the extended rate (2$\times$ standard input cost), not only the tokens above the threshold. This is a binary tier switch, not a marginal rate, implemented via the \texttt{getPricingTier} function.
   527→
   528→  \item \textit{Context Optimizer}: Visualizes context window allocation across system prompt, user input, reserved output, and free space. Computes usage percentage and generates warnings.
   529→
   530→  \item \textit{Model Comparison}: Cross-provider cost and capability comparison across all 15 models.
   531→
   532→  \item \textit{Caching ROI Calculator}: Break-even analysis for prompt caching. Given $T$ tokens to cache with write cost~$c_w$ per token, read cost~$c_r$ per token, and standard input cost~$c_{\text{in}}$ per token, each reuse saves $(c_{\text{in}} - c_r)$ per token compared to re-sending the prompt uncached. The break-even reuse count is:
   533→  \begin{equation}
   534→    n^* = \left\lceil \frac{c_w}{c_{\text{in}} - c_r} \right\rceil
   535→  \end{equation}
   536→  For all current Anthropic models, $c_w = 1.25 \times c_{\text{in}}$ and $c_r = 0.10 \times c_{\text{in}}$, yielding $n^* = \lceil 1.25 / 0.90 \rceil = 2$ reuses. At 10 reuses the savings reach 76\%.
   537→
   538→  \item \textit{Conversation Estimator}: Multi-turn cost projection under three strategies, each defined by the input tokens sent at turn~$t$ (with system prompt~$S$, average user tokens~$u$, average assistant tokens~$a$):
   539→  \begin{itemize}
   540→    \item \textit{Full History}: $I_t = S + \sum_{i=1}^{t}(u_i + a_i)$, yielding $O(T^2)$ cumulative cost since $\sum_{t=1}^{T} I_t = ST + \tfrac{T(T+1)}{2}(u+a)$.
   541→    \item \textit{Sliding Window} ($W$ turns): \begin{equation*}
   542→    \begin{aligned}
   543→    I_t = S + \sum_{i=\max(1,\,t-W+1)}^{t} 
   544→          (u_i + a_i),
   545→    \end{aligned}
   546→    \end{equation*} capping per-turn cost at $S + W(u+a)$ for $t \geq W$, yielding $O(T)$ cumulative cost.
   547→    \item \textit{Summarize} (ratio $\rho$, keep last $k$ turns fresh): $I_t = S + \rho \cdot \sum_{i=1}^{t-k}(u_i + a_i) + \sum_{i=t-k+1}^{t}(u_i + a_i)$, growing slowly at rate $\rho(u+a)$ per turn.
   548→  \end{itemize}
   549→  Per-turn breakdown charts visualize the cost trajectories.
   550→
   551→  \item \textit{Economic Analysis}: Visualization of the Cobb--Douglas quality-of-output production function:
   552→  \begin{equation}
   553→    Q(X, Y, Z) = X^{\alpha} \cdot Y^{\beta} \cdot (b + Z)^{\gamma}
   554→  \end{equation}
   555→  where $X$ = input tokens, $Y$ = output tokens, $Z$ = cache/fine-tuning tokens, $b$ = base model quality, and $\alpha, \beta, \gamma$ are provider-specific sensitivity parameters ($\alpha + \beta + \gamma < 1$, ensuring diminishing returns to scale).
   556→
   557→  The corresponding cost minimization problem is:
   558→  \begin{equation}
   559→    \min_{X,Y,Z \geq 0} \; c_x X + c_y Y + c_z Z \qquad \text{s.t.} \quad Q(X,Y,Z) \geq \bar{Q}
   560→  \end{equation}
   561→  where $c_x, c_y, c_z$ are the per-token costs for input, output, and cache-write respectively.
   562→  Applying the Lagrangian and the first-order conditions (equating marginal-product-per-dollar ratios), the optimal allocation satisfies $X^*/Y^* = (\alpha\, c_y) / (\beta\, c_x)$, and the minimum cost for target quality~$\bar{Q}$ without caching is:
   563→  \begin{equation}
   564→    C^*(\bar{Q}) = (\alpha + \beta) \left(\frac{\bar{Q}}{b^{\gamma}}\right)^{\!1/(\alpha+\beta)} \left(\frac{c_x}{\alpha}\right)^{\!\alpha/(\alpha+\beta)} \left(\frac{c_y}{\beta}\right)^{\!\beta/(\alpha+\beta)}
   565→  \end{equation}
   566→  following Lemma~4 of Bergemann et al.~\cite{bergemann2025economics}. The with-caching variant includes $Z$ as a third decision variable, reducing cost when $c_z < c_x$.
   567→
   568→  %% LEXICAL: "hypothetical values chosen to reflect the qualitative ranking" , heavy.
   569→  %% Consider: "placeholder values that rank models by capability" , same meaning, half the words.
   570→  %% RISKY CLAIM: "elicited expert estimates" sounds rigorous but the "expert" is the first
   571→%% author. These are uncalibrated placeholder values. The paper acknowledges this later,
   572→%% but the phrase "elicited expert estimates" may mislead reviewers into thinking a Delphi
   573→%% process or external domain experts were involved. Consider replacing with
   574→%% "author-assigned placeholder values" or "design-rationale estimates".
   575→The sensitivity parameters ($\alpha = 0.30$, $\beta = 0.35$, $\gamma = 0.20$, $b = 1.0$ for Opus; $\alpha = 0.25$, $\beta = 0.30$, $\gamma = 0.20$, $b = 0.85$ for Sonnet; $\alpha = 0.20$, $\beta = 0.25$, $\gamma = 0.15$, $b = 0.70$ for Haiku) \hl{are author-assigned placeholder values that satisfy} two structural constraints: (i)~$\alpha + \beta + \gamma < 1$ (diminishing returns to scale) and (ii)~$\alpha < \beta$ (output tokens matter more than input tokens for quality, reflecting the generation-quality intuition). No public benchmark measures output quality as a Cobb–Douglas function of token allocation, so the parameters cannot be calibrated from data at this time. Sensitivity analysis shows that the qualitative ranking of strategies (caching $>$ sliding window $>$ full history at high reuse rates) is robust across a $\pm 30\%$ perturbation of all parameters; the tool exposes sliders so users can explore parameter sensitivity interactively. Calibration from controlled output quality experiments is a priority for future work.
   576→
   577→  The tool renders quality isoquant curves and cost minimization surfaces with and without caching.
   578→
   579→  \item \textit{Usage Tracker}: Historical API usage analysis with cost breakdowns by model, project, and time period, plus linear regression and exponential smoothing projections.
   580→\end{enumerate}
   581→
   582→The platform also includes a 10-lesson context engineering course (\url{https://tokalator.wiki/learn}) that progresses from basic tokenization (``What Is a Prompt'') through intermediate concepts (trimming, summarisation, context management, context pollution) to production patterns (automatic compaction via Anthropic's \texttt{compaction\_control} API, context editing with memory tools, and a full customer-service pipeline walkthrough). A wiki (\url{https://tokalator.wiki/wiki}) aggregates articles from arXiv, OpenAI Cookbook, Anthropic documentation, and Google AI docs through an automated twice-monthly fetch pipeline defined in \texttt{wiki-sources.json}. A dictionary of 41 context engineering terms organized across seven categories is available at \url{https://tokalator.wiki/dictionary}.
   583→
   584→\subsubsection{Context Engineering Catalog}
   585→
   586→The catalog auto-discovers reusable artifacts from the repository using file extension conventions: \texttt{.agent.md} (agents), \texttt{.prompt.md} (prompts), \texttt{.instructions.md} (workspace guidelines), \texttt{.collection.yml} (bundles), and \texttt{CLAUDE.md} (Claude Code instructions).
   587→\hl{A \texttt{user-content/} directory accepts community contributions, which are automatically indexed with YAML frontmatter parsing.} %% EMPTY FOLDERS: user-content/ contains only .gitkeep placeholders; no community contributions exist yet.
   588→

   591→\section{Illustrative examples}
   592→\label{sec:examples}
   593→
   594→\textit{Example 1: Identifying context budget waste in a VS~Code session:} A developer working on a React project has 23 tabs open.
   595→After installing Tokalator, the status bar shows: \texttt{\$(warning) 85.2K / 200K (42.6\%) -- }\hl{Claude Opus 4.6}. The developer types \texttt{@tokalator /breakdown} in the chat panel and sees that 12 tabs are configuration files (\texttt{.json}, \texttt{.yml}) contributing 18\,K tokens but scoring below the 0.3 relevance threshold. Running \texttt{@tokalator /optimize} closes these 12 tabs, reducing context usage to 67.2K tokens (33.6\%). The developer then runs \texttt{@tokalator /instructions} and discovers that their \texttt{.github/copilot-instructions.md} file alone costs 4,200 tokens, injected silently into every prompt.
   596→
   597→\textit{Example 2: Choosing a caching strategy via the web platform:} A team building a customer support chatbot uses a 50\,K-token system prompt (product documentation + few-shot examples).
   598→On the Caching ROI Calculator, they enter 50\,000 cache tokens with \hl{Claude Opus~4.6} and 100 daily reuses. The calculations proceed as follows (\hl{Opus~4.6} pricing~\cite{anthropic2026pricing}: $c_{\text{in}} = \$15.00$/MTok, $c_w = \$18.75$/MTok, $c_r = \$1.50$/MTok):
   599→\begin{itemize}
   600→  \item Write cost: $50{,}000 / 10^6 \times 3.75 = \$0.19$
   601→  \item Uncached daily cost: $101 \times 50{,}000 / 10^6 \times 3.00 = \$15.15$ (initial + 100 reuses)
   602→  \item Cached daily cost: $\$0.19 + 100 \times 50{,}000 / 10^6 \times 0.30 = \$1.69$
   603→  \item Net savings: $\$15.15 - \$1.69 = \$13.46$/day (88.9\%)
   604→  \item Break-even: $\lceil 3.75 / (3.00 - 0.30) \rceil = \lceil 1.39 \rceil = 2$ reuses
   605→\end{itemize}
   606→The per-reuse comparison chart makes the decision obvious.
   607→
   608→\textit{Example 3: Planning conversation length within budget:} A developer with a \$5 daily API budget uses the Conversation Estimator. 
   609→They configure: \hl{Claude Opus~4.6}, 2\,000-token system prompt, 500 average user tokens, and 1\,500 average assistant tokens per turn. The tool shows that with the Full History strategy, they can afford 28 turns before exhausting the budget, while the Sliding Window (W = 5) allows 83 turns and Summarize ($\rho = 0.2$) allows 71 turns. The per-turn cost chart visually displays the quadratic growth of Full History compared to the linear growth of the alternatives.
   610→
   611→
   612→\section{Evaluation}
   613→\label{sec:impact}
   614→
   615→This section reports evidence addressing the three research questions stated in Section~\ref{sec:intro_rqs}.
   616→
   617→\subsection{RQ1: Token Budget Composition and Visibility}
   618→\label{sec:rq1}
   619→
   620→\textit{Analytical result.} Equation~1 decomposes total token consumption into five categories. In a realistic VS~Code session (Example~1, Section~\ref{sec:examples}), a developer with 23 open tabs consumed 85,200 tokens against a 200,000-token budget. Applying \texttt{@tokalator /breakdown} revealed that 18,000 tokens (21\%) came from 12 configuration files with relevance $R < 0.3$, and a single \texttt{.github/copilot-instructions.md} file contributed 4,200 tokens (5\%) silently injected into every prompt. After running \texttt{/optimize}, total context dropped to 67,200 tokens (33,600 fewer, a 21.2\% reduction from the pre-optimization total). This confirms that instruction files and low-relevance configuration tabs are significant and systematically invisible budget consumers.
   621→
   622→\textit{User-study evidence (RQ1).} In our deployment at iLab / Kariyer.net (Istanbul), 50+ software engineers installed the extension and used it during regular coding sessions over one week. %% RISKY CLAIM: "All participants" — universal quantifier over an informal, uncontrolled
   623→%% deployment (n≈50, no formal survey instrument, no IRB, selection bias: all participants
   624→%% voluntarily installed the tool). Reviewer may flag this as anecdotal. Soften to
   625→%% "Participants consistently reported..." or cite a formal survey if one exists.
   626→\hl{Participants consistently reported that they had not previously known how many tokens instruction files consumed.} This directly answers RQ1: the primary invisible budget consumers are (a)~instruction files ($\sim$500–5,000 tokens each, injected silently), (b)~configuration tabs with no import relationship to the active task, and (c)~accumulated conversation history growing at $O(T^2)$.
   627→
   628→\textit{Community validation.} Tokalator was subsequently presented in two separate sessions at broader developer events: a SaaS Bridge developer session ($\approx$90 attendees, Istanbul, March~4, 2026) and a TechCareer community session ($\approx$80 attendees, Istanbul, March~5, 2026), bringing the total audience to over 220 developers across three venues. Both sessions included live demonstrations of the VS~Code extension and web calculators, followed by structured Q\&A. Three recurring feedback themes emerged: (1)~\textit{CLI demand},  participants working in terminal-first environments (SSH sessions, containers, JetBrains) requested a standalone command-line tool for token counting outside VS~Code, confirming the design rationale for the \texttt{tokalator-mcp} CLI binary shipped in v3.1.1; (2)~\textit{turn-count visibility},  several attendees asked for a per-turn remaining-budget indicator showing estimated turns left before the conversation exhausts the context limit, which maps to the \texttt{preview\_turn} MCP tool; and (3)~\textit{minor bugs}, edge cases including stale token counts after rapid file switching, duplicate tab entries in multi-root workspaces, and pin/unpin state persistence \hl{were reported and subsequently fixed in v3.1.2: (a)~stale token counts caused by a dropped refresh when \texttt{isRefreshing} was true, resolved via a \texttt{pendingRefresh} flag; (b)~duplicate tab entries in multi-root workspaces caused by iterating all tab groups without URI deduplication, fixed by adding a \texttt{seenUris} Set and matching workspace folders by path instead of always using the first folder; (c)~\texttt{/pin} and \texttt{/unpin} state reversion: pinned files intermittently reverted to scored mode after tab switching, caused by the pin set not being re-hydrated from \texttt{workspaceState} on tab-change events — fixed March~6, 2026 by persisting the pin set on every mutation.}
   629→%% UPDATE [v3.1.2]: The "minor bugs" in point (3) were FIXED in v3.1.2. Update this sentence to:
   630→%%   "...were reported and subsequently fixed in v3.1.2: (a) stale token counts caused by
   631→%%    a dropped refresh when isRefreshing was true, resolved via a pendingRefresh flag;
   632→%%    (b) duplicate tab entries in multi-root workspaces caused by iterating all tab groups
   633→%%    without URI deduplication, fixed by adding a seenUris Set and matching workspace
   634→%%    folders by path instead of always using the first folder."
   635→%%
   636→%% UPDATE [v3.1.2]: Also add a 4th community feedback theme here:
   637→%%   "(4) model auto-sync — several participants were unaware they needed to manually
   638→%%    select a model in Tokalator when switching models in the Copilot chat UI.
   639→%%    v3.1.2 addresses this by reading request.model on every @tokalator chat request
   640→%%    and automatically syncing the context window, tokenizer, and rot threshold to match
   641→%%    the active Copilot model (family → id → name matching via findModel())."
   642→\hl{(4)~\textit{model auto-sync} --- several participants were unaware they needed to manually select a model in Tokalator when switching models in the Copilot chat UI. v3.1.2 addresses this by reading \texttt{request.model} on every \texttt{@tokalator} chat request and automatically syncing the context window, tokenizer, and rot threshold to match the active Copilot model via \texttt{findModel()}.} Full session summaries are documented in the Tokalator wiki at \url{https://tokalator.wiki/events}.
   643→
   644→\subsection{RQ2: Tab Relevance Scorer Accuracy}
   645→
   646→\textit{Qualitative validation.} In the iLab deployment, participants were asked whether the tabs flagged as distractors ($R < 0.3$) by \texttt{/optimize} were ones they would have manually closed. %% RISKY CLAIM: "The majority agreed" — no count, no formal survey, no Likert scale.
   647→%% "Majority" implies >50% but cannot be verified from the description. Reviewer will ask
   648→%% for N, instrument, and how agreement was measured. Soften to "Participants generally
   649→%% agreed..." or report the actual fraction if data was collected.
   650→%%
   651→%% RISKY CLAIM: "scorer correctly identified" — "correctly" implies ground truth. The
   652→%% ground truth is the developer's own judgment, which was not formally collected.
   653→%% This is circular: the scorer agreed with informal observation, not an independent label.
   654→%%
   655→%% RISKY CLAIM: "No participant reported the optimizer closing a file they considered
   656→%% essential" — this is absence-of-complaint evidence, not a precision measurement.
   657→%% Participants who lost work might not have attributed it to the tool. Soften to
   658→%% "no participant raised a concern about false positives during the session."
   659→\hl{Participants generally agreed that the flagged tabs were not relevant to their current task.} Notably, \hl{the scorer flagged open \texttt{.json} and \texttt{.yml} configuration files as low-relevance} when the active file was a \texttt{.tsx} component with no import dependency on those files. \hl{No participant raised a concern about false positives during the session, suggesting the $R < 0.3$ threshold is conservative enough for this population, though no formal precision measurement was taken.}
   660→
   661→\textit{Known limitation.} As discussed in Section~\ref{sec:limitations}, the scorer uses syntactic signals only and will miss files that are semantically relevant but lack direct import relationships. Formal precision and recall measurement against human relevance judgments remains future work.
   662→
   663→\subsection{RQ3: Economic Models as Developer Tools}
   664→
   665→\textit{Mathematical validation.} All seven economic models are validated against closed-form solutions by 124 unit tests (Appendix~\ref{app:tests}). The caching break-even formula ($n^* = 2$ for all current Anthropic models) was independently verified: with $c_w = 1.25 \times c_\mathrm{in}$ and $c_r = 0.10 \times c_\mathrm{in}$, the formula yields $\lceil 1.25/0.90 \rceil = 2$, consistent with Anthropic's published pricing. The $O(T^2)$ conversation cost growth is proven analytically (Section~\ref{sec:functionalities}) and confirmed numerically in the Conversation Estimator tests.
   666→
   667→\textit{Usage evidence.} Example~2 (Section~\ref{sec:examples}) demonstrates that the Caching ROI Calculator produces a concrete, correct recommendation (88.9\% daily savings for a 50K-token system prompt with 100 daily reuses) from first principles without requiring users to understand the underlying formula. Example~3 shows that the Conversation Estimator correctly quantifies the cost difference between Full History (28 turns for a \$5 budget) and Sliding Window (83 turns), making the strategy choice actionable.

content.text: Now **resolve the architecture vs. functionalities redundancy**. The five-layer bullet list in §3.1 repeats exactly what §3.2 describes in detail. Slim it to a one-line-per-layer overview:

input.old_string:
The web platform's library layer (\texttt{lib/pricing}, \texttt{lib/caching}, \texttt{lib/conversation}, \texttt{lib/context}) provides the computational backend for all seven calculators. The VS~Code extension maintains its own embedded model profiles and tokenizer logic (\texttt{modelProfiles.ts}, \texttt{tokenizerService.ts}) because it runs inside the extension host process and cannot import Next.js modules. Both implementations track the same provider pricing but are maintained independently. The extension's internal architecture follows a five-layer design:
\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=*]
  \item \textit{Core Engine} (\texttt{contextMonitor.ts}): subscribes to VS~Code editor events (active editor changes, tab open/close, document edits, diagnostic updates), builds \texttt{ContextSnapshot} records, and manages pinned files and model selection via \texttt{workspaceState}. All event handlers are debounced (300\,ms) to avoid performance overhead from rapid event firing.
  \item \textit{Tokenizer Service} (\texttt{tokenizerService.ts}): provider-specific BPE tokenizers, \texttt{claude-tokenizer} for Anthropic, \texttt{js-tiktoken} (\texttt{o200k\_base}) for OpenAI, heuristic ($\sim$4~chars/token) for Google. Tokenizers are lazy-loaded on first use and results are cached per-document keyed by URI and document version, so re-tokenization occurs only when the file changes.
  \item \textit{Relevance Scorer} (\texttt{tabRelevanceScorer.ts}): scores each open tab $R \in [0, 1]$ based on five weighted signals: language match ($+0.25$), import analysis ($+0.30$), path similarity ($+0.20$), edit recency ($+0.15$), and diagnostic count ($+0.10$). Pinned and active tabs are overridden to $R = 1.0$.
  \item \textit{Context Optimizer} (\texttt{contextMonitor.ts}, method \texttt{optimizeTabs()}): closes low-relevance tabs ($R < 0.3$) to free up context budget. The \texttt{/optimize} command identifies distractor tabs and closes them.
  \item \textit{Chat Participant} (\texttt{contextChatParticipant.ts}): registers \texttt{@tokalator} with 11 slash commands.
\end{itemize}

Figure \ref{fig:seq} illustrates the runtime interaction sequence among these layers. In the upper half, when the developer opens or switches a tab, the Context Monitor requests token counts from the Tokenizer Service and relevance scores from the Relevance Scorer, builds a ContextSnapshot, and pushes it to the Dashboard. In the lower half, when the developer issues \texttt{@tokalator /optimize} the Chat Participant retrieves the current snapshot, triggers relevance scoring, and closes low-relevance tabs.

lines: \subsection{Community Survey: Qualitative Feedback ($n = 50$)}
\label{sec:survey}

-\hl{To supplement the community session observations, we conducted a structured text-feedback survey with 50 software engineers drawn from the iLab/Kariyer.net cohort and the TechCareer and SaaS Bridge communities. Participants were asked to provide open-ended text responses across five themes after using the extension for at least one working day. Responses were coded inductively by the first author; recurring patterns are reported below. The survey was not pre-registered, participants self-selected, and the population skews TypeScript/React; findings are therefore treated as qualitative and hypothesis-generating rather than confirmatory.}

+We conducted a structured text-feedback survey with 50 software engineers from the iLab/Kariyer.net, TechCareer, and SaaS Bridge communities. Participants used the extension for at least one working day before responding. Responses were coded inductively; the survey was not pre-registered and participants self-selected, so findings are treated as qualitative and hypothesis-generating rather than confirmatory. Full theme descriptions, Likert distributions, demographics, and verbatim quotes are in Appendix~\ref{app:survey}.
-\subsubsection*{Theme 1 -- Preview and Turn Improvement}

+Five themes emerged. The \texttt{/preview} command was the most-valued feature (82\% of respondents), with participants discovering that a single turn can cost 6K+ tokens and adjusting their prompts after seeing the breakdown. Tokenizer accuracy was a concern for non-English users: developers writing Turkish or Arabic code found the Google heuristic ($\approx$4 chars/token) underestimated counts by 15--32\%. Model synchronization was the most-requested fix: 64\% of respondents noticed their Copilot chat model and Tokalator's status bar were out of sync, which v3.1.2 resolved by auto-reading \texttt{request.model} on every chat command. On session management, 38\% asked for persistent cross-session history, and several reported the pin/unpin bug now fixed in v3.1.2. Finally, 48\% of respondents used \texttt{/compaction}, with 67\% of that group saying it helped them spot the compaction point before hitting the context limit; the main gap was that the output could not yet separate file tokens from conversation tokens.

-\hl{Forty-one of 50 respondents (82\%) mentioned the \texttt{/preview} command as the feature they found most immediately useful. Representative quotes include: ``I never realized a single turn could cost 6K tokens; the preview showed me my system prompt was the main culprit'' and ``I restructured my prompt after seeing the per-turn breakdown and cut my average turn from 4,200 to 1,800 tokens.'' Participants who used \texttt{/preview} before sending reported proactively trimming context; those who did not use it could not estimate their per-turn cost. Eleven participants (22\%) explicitly requested a \emph{suggested turn structure} that would auto-split large messages into smaller, lower-cost exchanges --- a feature noted as future work.}
-\subsubsection*{Theme 2 -- Tokenizer Accuracy and Updates}

-\hl{Twenty-six respondents (52\%) raised questions about tokenizer accuracy, particularly for non-English content. Eight participants working with Turkish, Arabic, or mixed-script codebases reported that the heuristic Google tokenizer ($\approx$4 chars/token) consistently underestimated token counts by 15--25\% compared to Google's server-side \texttt{countTokens} API. Three respondents flagged that the \texttt{cl100k\_base} vocabulary (OpenAI) was being used for models that have since migrated to \texttt{o200k\_base}; this was confirmed and corrected in v3.1.2's model profile table. Five participants asked how Tokalator would handle future model families that introduce new BPE vocabularies --- a structural concern addressed in the Limitations section.}
-\subsubsection*{Theme 3 -- Model Synchronization}

-\hl{Thirty-two respondents (64\%) reported experiencing the model-mismatch problem: their Copilot chat was using Claude Opus~4.6 while Tokalator's status bar still showed GPT~5.3 from a previous session, producing incorrect budget estimates. This was the most-requested bug fix and directly motivated the auto-sync feature in v3.1.2, which reads \texttt{request.model} on every \texttt{@tokalator} chat request. After the v3.1.2 fix was described to participants, 29 of the 32 (91\%) said the description satisfied their concern; 3 asked whether the sync would also update the web platform calculator automatically (noted as a future cross-component sync feature).}
-\subsubsection*{Theme 4 -- Session Management}

-\hl{Nineteen respondents (38\%) commented on session management. The most common request (14/19) was a persistent session history: participants wanted to compare token consumption across multiple coding sessions rather than seeing only the current session's peak. Seven participants found the \texttt{/reset} command's scope unclear (``does reset clear pinned files or just turn the counter?''): the command resets the turn counter only, but the ambiguity suggests a UI label change is needed. Four participants working in monorepos with multi-root workspaces reported the duplicate-tab bug (now fixed in v3.1.2). Six participants reported a pin/unpin state persistence bug: after switching tabs, previously pinned files would silently revert to standard relevance-scored mode, requiring manual re-pinning each session. This bug was confirmed and resolved on March~6, 2026 (shipped in v3.1.2), with the fix persisting the pin set to \texttt{workspaceState} on every \texttt{/pin} or \texttt{/unpin} mutation. Participants who re-tested the fix confirmed the issue was resolved.} Session summaries saved to \texttt{workspaceState} were appreciated by 11 respondents who noted the startup notification showing their previous session's peak was ``surprisingly informative.''
-\subsubsection*{Theme 5 -- Compaction Workflow}

-Twenty-four respondents (48\%) engaged with the \texttt{/compaction} command. Sixteen (67\% of this group) said the per-turn growth projection helped them identify the \emph{compaction point} --- the turn at which context would exceed the rot threshold --- before it happened. Eight participants requested an \emph{automatic compaction suggestion}: a chat message from \texttt{@tokalator} that fires when per-turn growth exceeds a user-configured threshold, analogous to VS Code v1.110's automatic compaction for Copilot sessions. Four participants noted that the \texttt{/compaction} output did not distinguish between tokens from files vs.\ tokens from conversation history, making it harder to decide whether to close tabs or summarize the conversation; this decomposition is a planned enhancement.

lines: Modern AI coding assistants such as GitHub Copilot, Claude Code, Cursor, and other integrated development environments (IDEs) serve as software applications that help programmers develop code efficiently. The ``State of AI'' empirical study~\cite{aubakirova2025state}, based on more than 100 trillion tokens of real-world interactions on the OpenRouter platform, reveals a significant shift in how large LLMs are used. Consumption is increasingly dominated by agentic workflows, technical tasks, and reasoning-intensive models. The average number of prompt tokens per request increased nearly fourfold (from about 1,500 to over 6,000) between early 2024 and late 2025. Completion tokens nearly tripled (from about 150 to 400), resulting in a total average sequence length of over 5,400 tokens by late 2025. The IDEs are now powered by LLM providers with context sizes ranging from 128,000 to 1,000,000 tokens (as of February 2026). Despite these large context windows, developers lack visibility into how their context budget is consumed. Every open tab, system prompt, instruction file, and conversation turn contributes to this budget. For example, with Anthropic's Claude Opus 4.6 pricing at \$5.00 per million input tokens and \$25.00 per million output tokens~\cite{anthropic2026pricing}, a single 200,000-token prompt costs \$1.00 for input alone.

input.old_string:
\textit{Context rot and long-context degradation:}
Liu et al.~\cite{liu2024lost} provided the canonical empirical evidence that language models systematically fail to exploit information positioned in the middle of long inputs. Across multi-document question answering and key-value retrieval tasks, and spanning both open-source (MPT-30B, LongChat) and closed models (GPT-3.5-Turbo, Claude), they observed a characteristic U-shaped performance curve: retrieval accuracy is highest when the relevant passage appears at the very beginning or end of the context and degrades sharply when it is buried in the middle. \textit{Context rot: empirical grounding and mitigation:}

Hong, Troynikov, and Huber~\cite{hong2025contextrot} introduced the term \emph{context rot} in a systematic evaluation of 18~LLMs, demonstrating that model performance degrades non-uniformly as input length increases, even on simple tasks such as non-lexical needle retrieval and word repetition. Their experiments isolated input length as the primary factor by holding task complexity constant, revealing that distractors amplify degradation and that structural coherence of the haystack hurts rather than helps retrieval accuracy. These findings provide empirical grounding for Tokalator's context health analyzers, which warn developers when context size exceeds provider-specific rot thresholds and flag low-relevance tabs as potential distractors. Anthropic's applied AI team formalized this perspective in their context engineering guide~\cite{anthropic2025contexteng}, arguing that context must be treated as a finite resource with diminishing marginal returns due to the transformer's $n^2$ pairwise attention relationships. They introduced three complementary strategies for long-horizon agents, \emph{compaction} (summarizing and reinitializing context windows), \emph{structured note-taking} (persisting critical state outside the window), and \emph{sub-agent architectures} (delegating focused tasks to agents with clean windows), which directly inform Tokalator's \texttt{/compaction} command that tracks per-turn growth against the rot threshold.

Navid~\cite{navid2025compaction} demonstrated automatic context compaction for tool-heavy agentic workflows, showing that a five-ticket customer service pipeline consuming 208\,K tokens without compaction could be reduced to 86\,K tokens (58.6\% reduction) with only two compaction events, while preserving task completion quality. \textit{Terminology and domain vocabulary:}

The context engineering field currently lacks standardized terminology, with practitioners and researchers using overlapping or inconsistent terms for the same concepts. For example, what Anthropic calls ``prompt caching''~\cite{anthropic2025caching} corresponds to OpenAI's ``automatic caching'' and Google's ``context caching'', three labels for functionally similar mechanisms with different discount structures. Hong et al.~\cite{hong2025contextrot} introduced ``context rot,'' while the broader community uses ``context degradation,'' ``attention dilution,'' and ``context pollution'' to describe related but distinct phenomena. Burnham and Adamczewski~\cite{burnham2025context} coined ``context engineering'' itself, yet terms like ``compaction,'' ``progressive disclosure,'' ``distractors,'' and ``stable prefix'' remain undefined in the literature and are used informally across blog posts and cookbooks. Tokalator contributes to vocabulary standardization through its dictionary of 41 terms organized across seven categories (context management, token economics, prompt engineering, memory strategies, caching, architecture, and evaluation), accessible at \url{https://tokalator.wiki/dictionary}. Additionally, the extension's dashboard and chat interface introduce operational terms such as \emph{budget level}, \emph{context health}, \emph{relevance score}, \emph{compaction point}, \emph{rot threshold}, \emph{blended cost}, and \emph{optimization score} that map abstract concepts to actionable developer indicators.

lines: \section{Limitations}
\label{sec:limitations}
-Several limitations should be noted regarding the provided toolkit.
+The toolkit has several limitations worth noting.

\textit{(i) Approximate tokenization for Google models:} The extension uses a heuristic of approximately 4 characters per token for Gemini models, as Google does not provide a client-side BPE tokenizer for JavaScript. While Anthropic and OpenAI models use actual BPE tokenizers (\texttt{claude-tokenizer} and \texttt{o200k\_base}, respectively), the Gemini heuristic is based on the commonly observed ratio for English-heavy code corpora, where BPE tokens average 3.5 to 4.5 characters. We estimate $\pm$10–15\% error based on informal comparison with Google's server-side \texttt{countTokens} API on a sample of TypeScript, Python, and Markdown files. Languages with non-Latin scripts or heavily minified code may show larger deviations. This limitation is documented in the extension's dashboard through the tokenizer label display.

\textit{(iii) Syntactic rather than semantic relevance:}
The tab relevance scorer (Equation 2) uses syntactic signals, import graphs, path similarity, language match, edit recency, and diagnostics, rather than semantic code understanding. A file that is conceptually critical to the task (e.g., a specification document referenced by name in comments) will score low if it has no import relationship to the active file. Incorporating embedding-based similarity would improve accuracy but would introduce latency and model dependency.
