\textbf{(3)~Semantic relevance scoring.} The syntactic five-signal scorer (Equation~2) misses files that are semantically related but lack import links (Section~\ref{sec:limitations}). Two complementary approaches from the literature are applicable: (a)~the EVOR framework of Shi et al.~\cite{shi2024evor} (arXiv:2402.12317), which iteratively refines retrieved context during code synthesis using evolving queries, could be adapted to dynamically re-rank open tabs as the active task evolves; (b)~the position-aware token-weighting scheme of Helm et al.~\cite{helm2025tokenweighting} (arXiv:2503.09202), which demonstrates that non-uniform loss weights improve long-context understanding, supports the theoretical motivation for scoring tabs by predicted contribution rather than recency. Both approaches would require embedding inference (e.g., a local ONNX model) to remain latency-compatible with the IDE.

lines: \hl{These figures demonstrate that AI-assisted development at the individual practitioner level is economically accessible: a commercially publishable, 20,814-LOC multi-component toolkit was constructed in 30 calendar days for a total net AI compute cost of \$28.36. 1→# Tokalator
     2→
     3→A context engineering toolkit for AI coding. Website + VS Code extension + reusable prompts
     4→
     5→**Site**: [tokalator.wiki](https://tokalator.wiki)
     6→**Extension**: [VS Code Marketplace](https://marketplace.visualstudio.com/items?itemName=vfaraji89.tokalator)
     7→
     8→---
     9→
    10→## Why
    11→
    12→AI assistants have finite context windows. When you have 30 tabs open, your assistant's attention gets diluted across irrelevant files. 
    13→You can't see what's happening -- how many tokens you're using, which files matter, when context rot starts to kick in.
    14→
    15→A set of calculators and tools for understanding AI token economics:
    16→
    17→- Token calculator with real-time pricing across updated models
    18→- Model comparison -- context windows, costs, capabilities side by side
    19→- Caching calculator for estimating prompt caching savings
    20→- Conversation estimator that predicts when context rot will hit
    21→- Context optimizer for building token budgets
    22→- A interactive course on context engineering
    23→- A wiki with +40 terms defined.
    24→
    25→## The Extension
    26→
    27→A VS Code sidebar that tracks your context budget in real time:
    28→
    29→- Shows token usage as LOW / MEDIUM / HIGH
    30→- Ranks open files by relevance to what you're actually working on
    31→- One click to close the noise
    32→- Pin important files so they're always counted
    33→- Chat commands via `@tokalator` — count, optimize, pin, breakdown, instructions, model
    34→
    35→Scores files based on language match, import relationships, path proximity, edit recency, and diagnostics.
    36→
    37→## Getting Started
    38→
    39→```bash
    40→# website
    41→git clone https://github.com/vfaraji89/tokalator.git
    42→cd tokalator && npm install && npm run dev
    43→
    44→# extension
    45→cd tokalator-extension-vs && npm install && npm run compile
    46→# then F5 in VS Code
    47→```
    48→
    49→## Structure
    50→
    51→The repo has three main parts:
    52→
    53→- `app/` and `components/` -- the Next.js website
    54→- `tokalator-extension-vs/` -- the VS Code extension
    55→- `copilot-contribution/` -- prompts, agents, and instructions you can drop into your own projects
    56→
    57→## Contributing
    58→
    59→Open an issue, submit a PR, or just drop prompt files into `user-content/`.
    60→
    61→## License
    62→
    63→MIT
    64→

Here is a full gap analysis against ESWA requirements, with prioritized recommendations:

---

## ESWA Fit Analysis

**Good news:** ESWA is a strong target for this paper. It accepts system/toolkit papers with real-world deployment, values practical application over pure theory, and your marketplace + user study data is exactly the kind of evidence they want.

**Acceptance rate: ~16%.** Here is what separates accepted papers from rejected ones, and where the current paper stands.

---

## Critical Issues (will cause desk rejection)

### 1. Citation style is wrong — must fix before submission
```latex
\usepackage[numbers]{natbib}   % current — numbered [1][2][3]
```
ESWA requires **author-year** style: `(Smith, 2023)` / `(Smith & Jones, 2023)` / `(Smith et al., 2023)`. Every in-text cite in the paper needs to become `\citep{}` or `\citet{}` and the natbib option changed:
```latex
\usepackage{natbib}   % remove [numbers]
\bibliographystyle{elsarticle-harv}   % or cas-model2-names with author-year
```
The bibliography format in `\bibliographystyle{cas-model2-names}` also needs to be checked — it must produce author-year output, not numbered output.

### 2. Document class needs to match ESWA template
The current `cas-dc` (double-column CAS) is used for some Elsevier journals but ESWA uses `elsarticle`. Download the official ESWA/Elsevier template from Overleaf (`elsarticle`) and migrate. The `cas-dc`-specific macros like `\shorttitle`, `\shortauthors`, `\cormark`, `\ead`, `\credit`, `\affiliation` may not all be supported identically.

### 3. Abstract contains LaTeX macros and internal comments
The abstract block currently has `\hl{...}` highlights, `%% EMPTY FOLDERS` inline comments, and math like `$n^* = 2$` and `$O(T^2)$`. For submission the abstract must be clean plain text (ESWA strips the PDF abstract for indexing). The inline `%% EMPTY FOLDERS` comment inside the abstract is also a content accuracy problem — the catalog numbers it describes are aspirational, not real.

---

## High-Priority Issues (will draw major revision requests)

### 4. No explicit Results and Discussion section
ESWA expects IMRaD structure. The current paper has:
- §3 Software description
- §4 Illustrative examples
- §5 Evaluation
- §6 Limitations
- §7 Conclusions

ESWA reviewers will look for a dedicated **Results & Discussion** section that interprets the findings, compares them to prior work, and states practical implications. The current §4 (Evaluation) mixes results with methodology. Recommended restructure:

| Current | Recommended for ESWA |
|---|---|
| §3 Software description | §3 System Design (keep) |
| §4 Illustrative examples | §4 Experimental Setup & Results |
| §5 Evaluation | §5 Discussion |
| §6 Limitations | §5.1 Limitations (subsection) |
| §7 Conclusions | §6 Conclusions |

### 5. Evaluation lacks a baseline comparison
ESWA reviewers expect: *"compared to what?"* The paper validates mathematics with 124 unit tests and reports a 21% context reduction, but there is no comparison to:
- Developing without Tokalator (control group)
- VS Code's native context indicator (v1.110)
- Manual tab management

Even a **Table comparing Tokalator workflow vs. unassisted workflow** on the 23-tab example (tokens before/after, decision time, cost) would satisfy this. The 50-person survey partially covers this but is not framed as a comparative evaluation.

### 6. No explicit "Practical Implications" subsection
ESWA explicitly values this. Add a short subsection (4–6 lines) in Discussion titled **Practical Implications for Development Teams** covering: when to enable caching, how to set relevance thresholds, recommended conversation strategies by budget.

### 7. Paper must be framed as an Intelligent/Expert System
ESWA's identity is "expert and intelligent systems applied in industry." The paper never uses these terms. Add to the Introduction:

> *Tokalator functions as an intelligent developer assistance system: it observes the IDE state, reasons about context budget health, and recommends or takes corrective actions — the core loop of any expert system applied to a software engineering task.*

Also frame the relevance scorer as a **knowledge-based inference engine** (it applies explicit rules to signals) and the economic calculators as a **decision support system**.

---

## Medium-Priority Issues (will draw minor revision requests)

### 8. Keyword format violations
ESWA: *"avoid multi-word expressions using 'and' or 'of'."*
Current keywords:
```
context engineering          ✓
token budget monitoring      ✓ (OK — no and/of)
LLM cost optimization        ✓
tab relevance scoring        ✓
Model Context Protocol       ✓
AI coding assistants         ✓
```
All 6 are fine. Consider replacing "AI coding assistants" with "intelligent development environments" to align with ESWA terminology.

### 9. Abstract length and clarity
Current abstract is ~210 words — within the 250-word limit. However, it lists four components as a numbered list which reads like a product spec, not a research abstract. ESWA's expected abstract structure:
1. **Problem** (1–2 sentences)
2. **Gap / motivation** (1 sentence)
3. **Proposed approach** (2–3 sentences — what the system does, not a feature list)
4. **Key results** (2–3 sentences with numbers)
5. **Conclusion / implication** (1 sentence)

### 10. The catalog count is a credibility risk
The abstract and three body locations claim "146+ agents, 140+ prompts, 161+ instruction files" but the actual repository has 1 agent, 3 prompts, 1 instruction in `copilot-contribution/` and an empty `user-content/`. If a reviewer checks the GitHub repo, this kills the paper. Options:
- State the **design capacity** and the current seed content honestly: *"The catalog accepts community contributions via standardized file conventions; the current repository includes an initial seed of community-curated artifacts."*
- Or if the scanner also walks `awesome-copilot/` (an external submodule), report those counts but be explicit about the source

### 11. Highlights file must be submitted separately
ESWA requires highlights as a **separate editable file** (not embedded in the LaTeX source using `\begin{highlights}`). The current 5 highlights bullets are good content — export them to a plain `.docx` or `.txt` file named `highlights.docx`.

---

## Structural Additions that Increase Acceptance

### Add: A system overview figure
ESWA papers almost always have a high-level architecture diagram in §3 showing the system as a whole. The current sequence diagram (Fig. 3) is too detailed for this role. Add a **1-page system overview figure** showing the four components (VS Code extension → Web Platform → Catalog → MCP Server) and their data flows.

### Add: A "Comparison with Baseline" table in §5
Even using the illustrative example data:

| Scenario | Without Tokalator | With Tokalator | Saving |
|---|---|---|---|
| 23-tab React session | 85.2K tokens | 67.2K tokens | 21.2% |
| 50K-token chatbot prompt (100 reuses/day) | \$15.15/day | \$1.69/day | 88.9% |
| \$5 budget, full-history strategy | 28 turns | 83 turns (sliding W=5) | 3× |

This gives reviewers the concrete "compared to what" they need.

### Add: Threats to Validity as a numbered subsection — not buried in Limitations
ESWA reviewers look for this explicitly. Move the current "Validity Threats" subsection out of §6 Limitations and make it **§5.x Threats to Validity** in the Discussion.

---

## Summary Checklist Before Submission

| Item | Status | Action |
|---|---|---|
| Citation style → author-year | ❌ Currently numbered | Change `[numbers]` option, update bib style |
| Document class → `elsarticle` | ⚠️ Using `cas-dc` | Migrate to ESWA template |
| Abstract clean of `\hl{}` and comments | ❌ Has macros + comments | Rewrite abstract as plain text |
| Abstract structure (Problem→Gap→Approach→Results) | ⚠️ Currently a feature list | Restructure |
| Catalog counts accurate | ❌ Inflated | Fix or reframe |
| Results & Discussion section | ❌ Missing | Add §5 Discussion |
| Practical Implications subsection | ❌ Missing | Add 6-line subsection |
| "Expert/intelligent system" framing | ❌ Not mentioned | Add to Introduction + §3 |
| Baseline comparison table | ❌ Missing | Add to Evaluation |
| Highlights as separate file | ⚠️ Embedded in LaTeX | Export to separate file |
| Threats to Validity as Discussion subsection | ⚠️ Buried in Limitations | Move to Discussion |
| Keywords ≤7, no "and"/"of" | ✅ 6 keywords, compliant | OK |
| Cover letter addressing ESWA scope | ❌ Not written | Write before submitting |

The biggest single risk is the **numbered citation style** — that alone can trigger a desk rejection on formatting grounds at many Elsevier journals. Fix that first.

# Expert Systems with Applications (ESWA) - Submission Information

## Review Timeline
- **First review round:** 5.6 months average
- **Total handling time:** 8.0 months for accepted manuscripts
- **Immediate rejection decision:** 10 days average
- **Average review rounds:** 1.9 rounds before final decision
- **Review reports per submission:** 2.3 reports average

## Review Quality Metrics
- **Quality of review reports:** 2.4/5.0 (below average)
- **Difficulty of reviewer comments:** 3.9/5.0 (difficult)
- **Overall manuscript handling rating:** 1.8/5.0 (poor)

## Author Experience Concerns
A recent submission received a highly critical assessment. The author reported: "Not all reviews are shared with authors (only some)" and described "questionable remarks" in decision-making. They noted concerns about ethical violations, including a reviewer requesting self-citations and subsequently rejecting the paper without proper justification when refused.

The author concluded the process lacked transparency and stated they would not resubmit to this journal.

## Missing Information
The journal has not provided editors' details about acceptance rates, desk rejection percentages, open access status, impact factors, or specific aims and scope criteria.

# Expert Systems with Applications - Journal Information

## Journal Overview
**Expert Systems with Applications** is published by Elsevier Ltd and covers artificial intelligence, computer science, and engineering applications. The journal maintains a Q1 ranking across multiple categories and publishes approximately 2,925 articles annually on a bimonthly schedule.

## Subject Focus
The journal addresses expert and intelligent systems across diverse fields: finance, accounting, engineering, marketing, law, risk assessment, medicine, human resources, and defense. It also publishes work on multi-agent systems, neural networks, knowledge management, and data mining applications.

## Submission & Review Insights

**From Reviewer Experiences:**

One author noted strong editorial practices: "The journal is very good in terms of the review process, the editorial board members, the chief editor, and the assignment of reviewers."

**Timeline Examples (User Reports):**
- One submission progressed from submission (June 24) to acceptance (August 26) with 30+ reviewer invitations and 6 reviewers providing feedback
- Another moved from submission to under review in 1 day, with 9 reviewers invited by day 2
- A third experienced slower progress, noting "Just a bit slow" after multiple status updates

**Common Questions:**
Authors asked about ORCID file requirements and email confirmation procedures for all co-authors, though specific answers weren't provided in available content.

## Notable Observations
Review turnaround times appear variable, with some submissions progressing rapidly while others extended several months despite multiple reviewer invitations.

\subsection*{Validity Threats}

\textit{(i) Internal validity.} The relevance score weights ($w_\mathrm{lang}=0.25$, $w_\mathrm{import}=0.30$, $w_\mathrm{path}=0.20$, $w_\mathrm{recency}=0.15$, $w_\mathrm{diag}=0.10$) were set by design reasoning, not measured against data. One source of bias is that the developer who chose the weights also observed the study participants, which may have skewed the evaluation. Future work should tune these weights against a held-out set of human relevance judgments.

\textit{(ii) Construct validity.} The extension estimates context consumption from open tabs, but the actual context construction of GitHub Copilot and Claude Code is proprietary. Consequently, the extension's token count is an upper-bound proxy, not a direct measurement. All reported figures (e.g., "21\% reduction") reflect estimated consumption, not confirmed API-level context size.

\textit{(iii) External validity.} The user study ran at three venues: Kariyer.net internal ($n \approx 50$), SaaS Bridge ($n \approx 90$), and TechCareer ($n \approx 80$), totalling $N > 220$ developers. The internal group shared a similar TypeScript/React stack; the community sessions had a wider mix of languages and roles. The results may not carry over to teams using compiled languages (C++, Rust), non-web domains, or different working styles. The sample is large enough to identify recurring feedback themes but not for statistical generalization.

\textit{(iv) Reliability.} The Cobb–Douglas sensitivity parameters ($\alpha$, $\beta$, $\gamma$) are placeholder values that satisfy structural constraints ($\alpha + \beta + \gamma < 1$) but are not calibrated from empirical data. Users who rely on the Economic Analysis tool for investment decisions should treat its outputs as directional rather than precise.

\subsection{RQ1: Token Budget Composition and Visibility}
\label{sec:rq1}

\textit{Analytical result.} Equation~1 decomposes total token consumption into five categories. In a realistic VS~Code session (Example~1, Section~\ref{sec:examples}), a developer with 23 open tabs consumed 85,200 tokens against a 200,000-token budget. Applying \texttt{@tokalator /breakdown} revealed that 18,000 tokens (21\%) came from 12 configuration files with relevance $R < 0.3$, and a single \texttt{.github/copilot-instructions.md} file contributed 4,200 tokens (5\%) silently injected into every prompt. After running \texttt{/optimize}, total context dropped to 67,200 tokens (33,600 fewer, a 21.2\% reduction from the pre-optimization total). This confirms that instruction files and low-relevance configuration tabs are significant and systematically invisible budget consumers.

\textit{User-study evidence (RQ1).} In our deployment at iLab / Kariyer.net (Istanbul), 50+ software engineers installed the extension and used it during regular coding sessions over one week. %% RISKY CLAIM: "All participants" — universal quantifier over an informal, uncontrolled
%% deployment (n≈50, no formal survey instrument, no IRB, selection bias: all participants
%% voluntarily installed the tool). Reviewer may flag this as anecdotal. Soften to
%% "Participants consistently reported..." or cite a formal survey if one exists.
\hl{Participants consistently reported that they had not previously known how many tokens instruction files consumed.} This directly answers RQ1: the primary invisible budget consumers are (a)~instruction files ($\sim$500–5,000 tokens each, injected silently), (b)~configuration tabs with no import relationship to the active task, and (c)~accumulated conversation history growing at $O(T^2)$.

\textit{Community validation.} Tokalator was subsequently presented in two separate sessions at broader developer events: a SaaS Bridge developer session ($\approx$90 attendees, Istanbul, March~4, 2026) and a TechCareer community session ($\approx$80 attendees, Istanbul, March~5, 2026), bringing the total audience to over 220 developers across three venues. Both sessions included live demonstrations of the VS~Code extension and web calculators, followed by structured Q\&A. Three recurring feedback themes emerged: (1)~\textit{CLI demand},  participants working in terminal-first environments (SSH sessions, containers, JetBrains) requested a standalone command-line tool for token counting outside VS~Code, confirming the design rationale for the \texttt{tokalator-mcp} CLI binary shipped in v3.1.1; (2)~\textit{turn-count visibility},  several attendees asked for a per-turn remaining-budget indicator showing estimated turns left before the conversation exhausts the context limit, which maps to the \texttt{preview\_turn} MCP tool; and (3)~\textit{minor bugs}, edge cases including stale token counts after rapid file switching, duplicate tab entries in multi-root workspaces, and pin/unpin state persistence \hl{were reported and subsequently fixed in v3.1.2: (a)~stale token counts caused by a dropped refresh when \texttt{isRefreshing} was true, resolved via a \texttt{pendingRefresh} flag; (b)~duplicate tab entries in multi-root workspaces caused by iterating all tab groups without URI deduplication, fixed by adding a \texttt{seenUris} Set and matching workspace folders by path instead of always using the first folder; (c)~\texttt{/pin} and \texttt{/unpin} state reversion: pinned files intermittently reverted to scored mode after tab switching, caused by the pin set not being re-hydrated from \texttt{workspaceState} on tab-change events — fixed March~6, 2026 by persisting the pin set on every mutation.}

\section{Introduction and Motivation}

Modern AI coding assistants such as GitHub Copilot, Claude Code, Cursor, and other integrated development environments (IDEs) serve as software applications that help programmers develop code efficiently. The ``State of AI'' empirical study~\cite{aubakirova2025state}, based on more than 100 trillion tokens of real-world interactions on the OpenRouter platform, reveals a significant shift in how large LLMs are used. Consumption is increasingly dominated by agentic workflows, technical tasks, and reasoning-intensive models. The average number of prompt tokens per request increased nearly fourfold (from about 1,500 to over 6,000) between early 2024 and late 2025. Completion tokens nearly tripled (from about 150 to 400), resulting in a total average sequence length of over 5,400 tokens by late 2025. The IDEs are now powered by LLM providers with context sizes ranging from 128,000 to 1,000,000 tokens (as of February 2026). Despite these large context windows, developers lack visibility into how their context budget is consumed. Every open tab, system prompt, instruction file, and conversation turn contributes to this budget. For example, with Anthropic's Claude Opus 4.6 pricing at \$5.00 per million input tokens and \$25.00 per million output tokens~\cite{anthropic2026pricing}, a single 200,000-token prompt costs \$1.00 for input alone.

+\section{Discussion}
+\label{sec:discussion}
+\subsection{Interpretation of Results}

+The three research questions share a common finding: token budget consumption in AI-assisted development is large, invisible by default, and highly manageable once made visible. The 21.2\% context reduction in Example~1 came entirely from removing files the developer had not intentionally included as context --- they were simply open tabs accumulated across a working session. Similarly, the 88.9\% daily cost saving in Example~2 was available to any team using a 50K-token system prompt, but only became actionable when the break-even calculation was presented concretely. These results suggest that the primary barrier to context efficiency is not developer motivation but information availability.

+The survey results reinforce this: 82\% of respondents named \texttt{/preview} as their most-valued feature, not because it changes what the model sees, but because it makes the cost of the next turn observable before it is incurred. This aligns with the broader literature on decision support systems: making a cost function explicit and real-time tends to shift behavior even without enforcement \citep{bergemann2025economics}.

+The model synchronization issue (64\% of users affected) highlights a structural gap in how current AI coding tools expose their state: developers switch models in the Copilot UI without any notification to companion tools. Tokalator's v3.1.2 auto-sync addresses this at the extension level, but a standard API for broadcasting active model changes across IDE extensions would benefit the entire ecosystem.
+\subsection{Practical Implications}
+For development teams adopting AI coding assistants, the findings from this work suggest four actionable guidelines:
+\begin{enumerate}[leftmargin=*]

+  \item \textit{Audit instruction files first.} A \texttt{CLAUDE.md} or \texttt{.github/copilot-instructions.md} file is injected silently into every prompt. A 4,000-token instruction file costs the same as 4,000 tokens of source code --- but applies to every single request. Teams should treat instruction files as high-ROI targets for context reduction.

+  \item \textit{Enable prompt caching for any system prompt used more than twice per day.} The break-even point for Anthropic models is two reuses. For OpenAI's automatic caching, the mechanism is always-on. Any team running a chatbot or agent with a fixed system prompt is losing money by not caching.

+  \item \textit{Use sliding-window or summarize strategies for conversations longer than 20 turns.} Full-history cost grows quadratically; switching to a 5-turn sliding window triples the number of affordable turns within the same daily budget (28 vs.\ 83 turns in Example~3).

+  \item \textit{Close distractor tabs before starting a coding session.} Configuration files (\texttt{.json}, \texttt{.yml}) open alongside active source files contribute tokens without providing useful context for most coding tasks. Running \texttt{@tokalator /optimize} at session start is a low-effort habit that reduces per-request cost immediately.
+\end{enumerate}
+\subsection{Threats to Validity}

+\textit{Internal validity.} The relevance score weights ($w_\mathrm{lang}=0.25$, $w_\mathrm{import}=0.30$, $w_\mathrm{path}=0.20$, $w_\mathrm{recency}=0.15$, $w_\mathrm{diag}=0.10$) were set by design reasoning, not measured against data. One source of bias is that the developer who chose the weights also observed the study participants, which may have skewed the evaluation. Future work should tune these weights against a held-out set of human relevance judgments.

+\textit{Construct validity.} The extension estimates context consumption from open tabs, but the actual context construction of GitHub Copilot and Claude Code is proprietary. The extension's token count is an upper-bound proxy, not a direct measurement. All reported figures (e.g., ``21\% reduction'') reflect estimated consumption, not confirmed API-level context size.

+\textit{External validity.} The user study ran at three venues: Kariyer.net internal ($n \approx 50$), SaaS Bridge ($n \approx 90$), and TechCareer ($n \approx 80$), totalling $N > 220$ developers. The internal group shared a similar TypeScript/React stack; the community sessions had a wider mix of languages and roles. The results may not carry over to teams using compiled languages (C++, Rust), non-web domains, or different working styles. The sample is large enough to identify recurring feedback themes but not for statistical generalization.

+\textit{Reliability.} The Cobb--Douglas sensitivity parameters ($\alpha$, $\beta$, $\gamma$) are placeholder values satisfying structural constraints ($\alpha + \beta + \gamma < 1$) but not calibrated from empirical data. Users relying on the Economic Analysis tool for investment decisions should treat its outputs as directional guidance, not precise predictions.
\section{Limitations}
\label{sec:limitations}

lines: \textit{(vii) Single-IDE scope:} The extension currently targets only VS~Code and GitHub Copilot. While the web platform is IDE-agnostic, the real-time context monitoring functionality does not extend to JetBrains IDEs, Neovim, or other editors. The architecture (TypeScript, VS~Code Extension API) would require a separate implementation effort for each target platform.
-\subsection*{Validity Threats}

-\textit{(i) Internal validity.} The relevance score weights ($w_\mathrm{lang}=0.25$, $w_\mathrm{import}=0.30$, $w_\mathrm{path}=0.20$, $w_\mathrm{recency}=0.15$, $w_\mathrm{diag}=0.10$) were set by design reasoning, not measured against data. One source of bias is that the developer who chose the weights also observed the study participants, which may have skewed the evaluation. Future work should tune these weights against a held-out set of human relevance judgments.

-\textit{(ii) Construct validity.} The extension estimates context consumption from open tabs, but the actual context construction of GitHub Copilot and Claude Code is proprietary. Consequently, the extension's token count is an upper-bound proxy, not a direct measurement. All reported figures (e.g., "21\% reduction") reflect estimated consumption, not confirmed API-level context size.

-\textit{(iii) External validity.} The user study ran at three venues: Kariyer.net internal ($n \approx 50$), SaaS Bridge ($n \approx 90$), and TechCareer ($n \approx 80$), totalling $N > 220$ developers. The internal group shared a similar TypeScript/React stack; the community sessions had a wider mix of languages and roles. The results may not carry over to teams using compiled languages (C++, Rust), non-web domains, or different working styles. The sample is large enough to identify recurring feedback themes but not for statistical generalization.

-\textit{(iv) Reliability.} The Cobb–Douglas sensitivity parameters ($\alpha$, $\beta$, $\gamma$) are placeholder values that satisfy structural constraints ($\alpha + \beta + \gamma < 1$) but are not calibrated from empirical data. Users who rely on the Economic Analysis tool for investment decisions should treat its outputs as directional rather than precise.

The 88.9\% cost saving from prompt caching is a known-achievable optimization that developers without a calculator consistently overlooked in our survey (only 12\% of respondents had calculated their caching break-even before using Tokalator).

\subsection{Community Survey: Qualitative Feedback ($n = 50$)}
\label{sec:survey}

We conducted a structured text-feedback survey with 50 software engineers from the iLab/Kariyer.net, TechCareer, and SaaS Bridge communities. Participants used the extension for at least one working day before responding. Responses were coded inductively; the survey was not pre-registered and participants self-selected, so findings are treated as qualitative and hypothesis-generating rather than confirmatory. Full theme descriptions, Likert distributions, demographics, and verbatim quotes are in Appendix~\ref{app:survey}.

Five themes emerged. The \texttt{/preview} command was the most-valued feature (82\% of respondents), with participants discovering that a single turn can cost 6K+ tokens and adjusting their prompts after seeing the breakdown. Tokenizer accuracy was a concern for non-English users: developers writing Turkish or Arabic code found the Google heuristic ($\approx$4 chars/token) underestimated counts by 15--32\%. 693→\section{Discussion}
   694→\label{sec:discussion}
   695→
   696→\subsection{Interpretation of Results}
   697→
   698→The three research questions share a common finding: token budget consumption in AI-assisted development is large, invisible by default, and highly manageable once made visible. The 21.2\% context reduction in Example~1 came entirely from removing files the developer had not intentionally included as context --- they were simply open tabs accumulated across a working session. Similarly, the 88.9\% daily cost saving in Example~2 was available to any team using a 50K-token system prompt, but only became actionable when the break-even calculation was presented concretely. These results suggest that the primary barrier to context efficiency is not developer motivation but information availability.
   699→
   700→The survey results reinforce this: 82\% of respondents named \texttt{/preview} as their most-valued feature, not because it changes what the model sees, but because it makes the cost of the next turn observable before it is incurred. This aligns with the broader literature on decision support systems: making a cost function explicit and real-time tends to shift behavior even without enforcement \citep{bergemann2025economics}.
   701→
   702→The model synchronization issue (64\% of users affected) highlights a structural gap in how current AI coding tools expose their state: developers switch models in the Copilot UI without any notification to companion tools. Tokalator's v3.1.2 auto-sync addresses this at the extension level, but a standard API for broadcasting active model changes across IDE extensions would benefit the entire ecosystem.
   703→
   704→\subsection{Practical Implications}
   705→
   706→For development teams adopting AI coding assistants, the findings from this work suggest four actionable guidelines:
   707→
   708→\begin{enumerate}[leftmargin=*]
   709→  \item \textit{Audit instruction files first.} A \texttt{CLAUDE.md} or \texttt{.github/copilot-instructions.md} file is injected silently into every prompt. A 4,000-token instruction file costs the same as 4,000 tokens of source code --- but applies to every single request. Teams should treat instruction files as high-ROI targets for context reduction.
   710→  \item \textit{Enable prompt caching for any system prompt used more than twice per day.} The break-even point for Anthropic models is two reuses. For OpenAI's automatic caching, the mechanism is always-on. Any team running a chatbot or agent with a fixed system prompt is losing money by not caching.
   711→  \item \textit{Use sliding-window or summarize strategies for conversations longer than 20 turns.} Full-history cost grows quadratically; switching to a 5-turn sliding window triples the number of affordable turns within the same daily budget (28 vs.\ 83 turns in Example~3).
   712→  \item \textit{Close distractor tabs before starting a coding session.} Configuration files (\texttt{.json}, \texttt{.yml}) open alongside active source files contribute tokens without providing useful context for most coding tasks. Running \texttt{@tokalator /optimize} at session start is a low-effort habit that reduces per-request cost immediately.
   713→\end{enumerate}
   714→
   715→\subsection{Threats to Validity}
   716→
   717→\textit{Internal validity.} The relevance score weights ($w_\mathrm{lang}=0.25$, $w_\mathrm{import}=0.30$, $w_\mathrm{path}=0.20$, $w_\mathrm{recency}=0.15$, $w_\mathrm{diag}=0.10$) were set by design reasoning, not measured against data. One source of bias is that the developer who chose the weights also observed the study participants, which may have skewed the evaluation. Future work should tune these weights against a held-out set of human relevance judgments.
   718→
   719→\textit{Construct validity.} The extension estimates context consumption from open tabs, but the actual context construction of GitHub Copilot and Claude Code is proprietary. The extension's token count is an upper-bound proxy, not a direct measurement. All reported figures (e.g., ``21\% reduction'') reflect estimated consumption, not confirmed API-level context size.
   720→
   721→\textit{External validity.} The user study ran at three venues: Kariyer.net internal ($n \approx 50$), SaaS Bridge ($n \approx 90$), and TechCareer ($n \approx 80$), totalling $N > 220$ developers. The internal group shared a similar TypeScript/React stack; the community sessions had a wider mix of languages and roles. The results may not carry over to teams using compiled languages (C++, Rust), non-web domains, or different working styles. The sample is large enough to identify recurring feedback themes but not for statistical generalization.
   722→
   723→\textit{Reliability.} The Cobb--Douglas sensitivity parameters ($\alpha$, $\beta$, $\gamma$) are placeholder values satisfying structural constraints ($\alpha + \beta + \gamma < 1$) but not calibrated from empirical data. Users relying on the Economic Analysis tool for investment decisions should treat its outputs as directional guidance, not precise predictions.
   724→
   725→\section{Limitations}
   726→\label{sec:limitations}
   727→
   728→The toolkit has several limitations worth noting.
   729→
   730→\textit{(i) Approximate tokenization for Google models:} The extension uses a heuristic of approximately 4 characters per token for Gemini models, as Google does not provide a client-side BPE tokenizer for JavaScript. While Anthropic and OpenAI models use actual BPE tokenizers (\texttt{claude-tokenizer} and \texttt{o200k\_base}, respectively), the Gemini heuristic is based on the commonly observed ratio for English-heavy code corpora, where BPE tokens average 3.5 to 4.5 characters. We estimate $\pm$10–15\% error based on informal comparison with Google's server-side \texttt{countTokens} API on a sample of TypeScript, Python, and Markdown files. Languages with non-Latin scripts or heavily minified code may show larger deviations. This limitation is documented in the extension's dashboard through the tokenizer label display.
   731→
   732→\textit{(ii) Extension performance overhead:} The extension subscribes to six VS Code event streams: active editor, tab changes, document edits, document open and close, diagnostics, and configuration changes. To prevent UI blocking, all event handlers use a 300 ms debounce timer, so at most one \texttt{refresh()} call occurs per 300 ms burst. Token counts are cached per document, keyed by URI and version number; re-tokenization occurs only when the document content changes. The BPE tokenizers are lazy-loaded (Claude ranks: 696\, KB JSON, o200k\_base: loaded via \texttt{js-tiktoken}), adding a one-time latency of approximately 100–200 ms on first use. A periodic background refresh (default 2 s, configurable) updates recency-based scores. In informal testing with over 30 open tabs,
   733→the extension contributes less than 5 ms per snapshot build after the initial tokenizer warm-up, which is imperceptible to the user.
   734→
   735→\textit{(iii) Syntactic rather than semantic relevance:}
   736→The tab relevance scorer (Equation~2) uses structural signals --- import graphs, path similarity, language match, edit recency, and diagnostics --- not semantic understanding. A file that is conceptually important (e.g., a design document referenced in comments) will score low if it has no import relationship to the active file. Embedding-based similarity would improve accuracy but would add latency and a model dependency.
   737→

\begin{frontmatter}

\title{Tokalator: A Context Engineering Toolkit for {AI} Coding Assistants}

\author[1]{Vahid Farajijobehdar\corref{cor1}}
\ead{vfaraji89@gmail.com}

\author[1]{\.{I}lknur K\"{o}seo\u{g}lu Sar{\i}}

\begin{abstract}
AI coding assistants such as GitHub Copilot, Claude Code, and Cursor operate within finite context windows of 128,000 to 1,000,000 tokens. When developers accumulate open files, instruction files, and long conversation histories, model attention degrades and API costs grow quadratically with session length. Yet no cross-provider, cost-modeling tool has previously made these costs visible inside the IDE. We present Tokalator, an open-source intelligent developer assistance system that addresses this gap through four components: a VS~Code extension that monitors token budgets in real time, scores open tabs by syntactic relevance using five signals, and closes distractor tabs on demand via 11 chat commands; a web platform with seven interactive calculators implementing closed-form caching break-even analysis, Cobb--Douglas quality optimization, and three conversation cost strategies with proven $O(T^2)$ growth for full-history sessions; a context engineering catalog of reusable agents, prompts, and instruction files; and a Model Context Protocol (MCP) server and CLI for Claude Code integration. The system covers 14 LLM models across three providers (Anthropic, OpenAI, Google) and is validated by 124 unit tests. A qualitative deployment study with 50 software engineers and community presentations to over 220 developers across three venues confirm that instruction files and low-relevance configuration tabs are the primary invisible budget consumers. In our illustrative example, Tokalator reduced context usage by 21.2\%; prompt caching analysis showed 88.9\% daily cost savings for a 50,000-token system prompt with 100 daily reuses. The VS~Code extension reached a 77.62\% page-to-acquisition conversion rate and 163 acquisitions within its first 30 days on the Marketplace.
\end{abstract}

\begin{keyword}
context engineering \sep token budget monitoring \sep LLM cost optimization \sep intelligent development environment \sep Model Context Protocol \sep decision support system
\end{keyword}

\end{frontmatter}

\begin{highlights}
\item Real-time VS~Code extension decomposes token budgets across five cost categories for 14 LLM models
\item Five-signal syntactic relevance scorer identifies distractor tabs and reduces context usage on demand
\item Closed-form caching break-even ($n^*=2$), $O(T^2)$ conversation cost proofs, and Cobb--Douglas quality optimization in interactive calculators
\item MCP server + CLI brings real Claude BPE token counting to Claude Code and any MCP-capable agent
\item Validated by 124 unit tests; 220+ developers across three community sessions
\end{highlights}


\section{Introduction and Motivation}

Modern AI coding assistants such as GitHub Copilot, Claude Code, Cursor, and other integrated development environments (IDEs) serve as software applications that help programmers develop code efficiently. The ``State of AI'' empirical study~\cite{aubakirova2025state}, based on more than 100 trillion tokens of real-world interactions on the OpenRouter platform, reveals a significant shift in how large LLMs are used. Consumption is increasingly dominated by agentic workflows, technical tasks, and reasoning-intensive models. The average number of prompt tokens per request increased nearly fourfold (from about 1,500 to over 6,000) between early 2024 and late 2025. Completion tokens nearly tripled (from about 150 to 400), resulting in a total average sequence length of over 5,400 tokens by late 2025. The IDEs are now powered by LLM providers with context sizes ranging from 128,000 to 1,000,000 tokens (as of February 2026). Despite these large context windows, developers lack visibility into how their context budget is consumed. Every open tab, system prompt, instruction file, and conversation turn contributes to this budget. For example, with Anthropic's Claude Opus 4.6 pricing at \$5.00 per million input tokens and \$25.00 per million output tokens~\cite{anthropic2026pricing}, a single 200,000-token prompt costs \$1.00 for input alone.

The rapid growth of agentic coding tools (GitHub Copilot, Claude Code, Cursor) makes this worse: Robbes et al.~\cite{robbes2026agentic} found 15.85--22.60\% adoption of coding agents across 129,134 GitHub projects, with agentic sessions consuming far more tokens per interaction than traditional completions. Han et al.~\cite{han2024talebudget} showed that token budgets can be enforced at the reasoning level, compressing chain-of-thought steps without significant quality loss, but no IDE tool previously exposed this budget control in a cross-provider, cost-modeling form (VS~Code~v1.110, released concurrently~\cite{vscode2026v110}, introduced a native context indicator scoped to Copilot sessions only).

Existing tools cover only parts of this problem: \texttt{tiktoken}~\cite{sennrich2016bpe} and Anthropic's tokenizer count tokens offline but have no IDE integration, no cross-provider support, and no cost modeling. Bergemann et al.~\cite{bergemann2025economics} built a formal economic framework for LLM output quality but did not turn it into a developer tool. Without integrated tooling, three problems arise:

\begin{enumerate}[leftmargin=*]
  \item \textit{Attention dilution}: irrelevant files compete with relevant ones for the context window, reducing model output quality~\cite{bergemann2025economics,hong2025contextrot}.
  \item \textit{Cost escalation}: conversations that send full history at every turn grow at $O(T^2)$ cumulative cost, because at turn~$t$ the model receives $S + t(u + a)$ input tokens (system prompt~$S$, average user tokens~$u$, average assistant tokens~$a$), so total input cost is $\sum_{t=1}^{T}[S + t(u+a)] = ST + \tfrac{T(T+1)}{2}(u+a) \in O(T^2)$.
  \item \textit{Context rot}: after 20+ turns, stale context hurts model accuracy; Hong et al.~\cite{hong2025contextrot} showed this degradation is uneven across models, appears even on simple retrieval tasks, and gets worse when distractor content is present.
\end{enumerate}

This paper addresses three research questions:\label{sec:intro_rqs}

\begin{description}
  \item[\textbf{RQ1}] \textit{What are the primary sources of token budget consumption in a typical AI-assisted development session, and can they be made visible to developers in real time?}
  \item[\textbf{RQ2}] \textit{Can a lightweight syntactic relevance scorer reliably identify distractor tabs that developers agree are not relevant to the current task?}
  \item[\textbf{RQ3}] \textit{Can formal economic models (Cobb--Douglas production functions, caching break-even analysis, conversation cost projections) be turned into practical developer tools without needing access to proprietary model internals?}
\end{description}

We present Tokalator, an intelligent developer assistance system that observes IDE state, reasons about context budget health, and recommends or takes corrective actions --- the core loop of an expert system applied to a software engineering task. Its relevance scorer acts as a knowledge-based inference engine (applying weighted rules over five observable signals), and its economic calculators form a decision support system that translates formal LLM cost models into actionable recommendations without requiring developers to work through the underlying mathematics. Tokalator makes the following contributions:
\begin{enumerate}[leftmargin=*]
  \item A \textit{real-time context budget monitor} integrated into VS~Code that decomposes token consumption across five categories (files, system prompt, instructions, conversation, output reservation) and raises health warnings based on provider-specific rot thresholds.
  \item A \textit{five-signal tab relevance scorer} that ranks open files by predicted contribution to the AI response and closes distractors on demand, reducing context usage by approximately 21\% in our illustrative example (Section~\ref{sec:examples}); broader deployment savings vary by project and tab management habits.
  \item \textit{Closed-form economic models} for caching break-even ($n^* = \lceil c_w / (c_\mathrm{in} - c_r) \rceil = 2$ for Anthropic models), conversation cost projection under three strategies, and Cobb–Douglas quality optimization, packaged in interactive web calculators.
  \item A \textit{Model Context Protocol (MCP) server and CLI} that brings the same BPE token counting directly into Claude Code and any MCP-capable agent.
  \item A \textit{context engineering catalog} with an open contribution structure: reusable agents, prompts, instruction files, and collections are auto-discovered from community-contributed directories using file-extension conventions; an initial seed of curated artifacts is included and the catalog grows with community submissions.
\end{enumerate}

\textit{Tokenization libraries:} OpenAI's \texttt{tiktoken} and Anthropic's \texttt{claude-tokenizer} provide programmatic token counting for their respective BPE vocabularies~\cite{sennrich2016bpe,openai2025cookbook}. Each provider uses a distinct encoding: OpenAI models use \texttt{cl100k\_base} or \texttt{o200k\_base}, while Anthropic models use their proprietary BPE vocabulary. Anthropic exposes a server-side token counting endpoint via the Messages API~\cite{anthropic2025tokencounting}; Tokalator replicates this client-side via \texttt{@anthropic-ai/tokenizer}, enabling offline, zero-API-call token counts. Neither library offers real-time IDE integration, multi-provider comparison, or cost estimation.

\textit{LLM pricing and inference economics:} Bergemann, Bonatti, and Smolin~\cite{bergemann2025economics} formalized LLM output quality as a Cobb–Douglas production function of input, output, and cached tokens, but did not provide an implementation. Erdil~\cite{erdil2025pareto} analyzed Pareto frontiers of inference cost versus capability, while Cottier et al.~\cite{cottier2025price} documented rapid but uneven price declines across tasks. Yotta Labs~\cite{yotta2026econ} examined inference economics beyond per-token pricing. These studies provide economic theory but no developer-facing tools.

\textit{Energy and environmental cost of inference:}
Beyond monetary pricing, LLM inference carries measurable energy and carbon costs that scale directly with token count. Lucchese et al.~\cite{lucchese2025energy} formally defined \emph{energy per token} ($E_{\text{tok}}$), showed how to measure it from GPU power traces, and demonstrated that models of similar parameter count can differ substantially in energy efficiency. Bannour et al.~\cite{bannour2025profiling} analyzed large-scale inference datasets and quantified a baseline energy coefficient of approximately $5.28 \times 10^{-7}$\,kWh per output token, with strong linear correlation between token length and energy consumption. Antonini et al.~\cite{antonini2025analytical} built a predictive model linking FLOPs, sequence lengths, and measured energy, formalizing $E_{\text{tok}} = E_{\text{tot}} / n_{\text{out}}$ as joules per output token. On the sustainability side, Sridhara et al.~\cite{sridhara2024sprout} (EMNLP 2024) showed a near-linear relationship between total carbon emissions and tokens generated for LLaMA-2 7B and 13B, and proposed SPROUT, a framework for carbon-efficient inference scheduling. Khowaja et al.~\cite{khowaja2025energy} introduced a taxonomy of ``energy-sensitive'' prompt elements and a Tokens-per-Joule metric for prompt optimization. Empirical measurements on 65B-class LLaMA models have reported $\sim$3--4\,J per output token on older GPU hardware~\cite{johnsnowlabs2026tpj}. Together, these studies establish that \emph{every token saved is simultaneously a cost saving and an emissions reduction}, providing an additional environmental rationale for Tokalator's budget monitoring and optimization features: by surfacing exact token counts and flagging low-relevance context, Tokalator enables developers to reduce both API spend and inference energy footprint.

\textit{Context window research:}
The ``State of AI'' study by Aubakirova et al.~\cite{aubakirova2025state} documented approximately a 4$\times$ increase in average prompt length on OpenRouter (from 1.5\,K to 6\,K tokens) between 2024 and 2025, driven by agentic workflows. Emberson et al.~\cite{emberson2025length} showed that LLM responses have been growing longer over time, further increasing context pressure. Fu et al.~\cite{fu2024scaling} demonstrated that data engineering choices (mixture ratios and sequence packing) critically determine whether models can exploit 128K context windows at all, reinforcing that context length is a resource to be managed, not merely maximized. Wei et al.~\cite{wei2025tokenweighting} proposed position-aware token weighting, showing that not all tokens in the context window contribute equally to generation quality, a finding that theoretically supports Tokalator's approach of scoring tabs by predicted contribution rather than treating all open files as equally valuable. Burnham and Adamczewski~\cite{burnham2025context} introduced the term ``context engineering'' to describe the systematic design of what enters the context window.

\textit{Context rot and long-context degradation:}
Liu et al.~\cite{liu2024lost} showed that language models systematically miss information placed in the middle of a long input. Across question answering and key-value retrieval tasks, using both open-source (MPT-30B, LongChat) and closed models (GPT-3.5-Turbo, Claude), they found a U-shaped accuracy curve: retrieval is best when the relevant passage is near the start or end of the context and drops sharply when it is buried in the middle. This means that a larger context window does not automatically mean better results --- a finding that directly motivates Tokalator's per-file relevance scorer, which ranks files by predicted contribution rather than by recency alone.

\textit{Context rot: evidence and mitigation:}
Hong, Troynikov, and Huber~\cite{hong2025contextrot} introduced the term \emph{context rot} in an evaluation of 18~LLMs, showing that model performance drops unevenly as input length grows, even on simple tasks like needle retrieval and word repetition. They kept task difficulty constant and varied only input length, finding that distractor content makes things worse and that a well-structured haystack does not help retrieval accuracy. These results back Tokalator's context health warnings, which alert developers when their context size passes a provider-specific rot threshold and flag low-relevance tabs as likely distractors. Anthropic's applied AI team took the same view in their context engineering guide~\cite{anthropic2025contexteng}, treating context as a limited resource with diminishing returns because of the transformer's $n^2$ attention cost. They described three strategies for long-running agents: \emph{compaction} (summarizing and restarting the context window), \emph{structured note-taking} (keeping critical state outside the window), and \emph{sub-agent architectures} (handing focused sub-tasks to agents with clean windows). These ideas directly shaped Tokalator's \texttt{/compaction} command.

\textit{Context compaction:}
Navid~\cite{navid2025compaction} demonstrated automatic context compaction for tool-heavy agentic workflows, showing that a five-ticket customer service pipeline consuming 208\,K tokens without compaction could be reduced to 86\,K tokens (58.6\% reduction) with only two compaction events, while preserving task completion quality. The technique monitors token usage per turn, injects a summary prompt when a threshold is exceeded, and replaces the conversation history with the compressed summary. Navid's cookbook provided both SDK-based compaction via Anthropic's \texttt{compaction\_control} parameter and a manual chat-loop pattern applicable to any conversational application. This work directly inspired Tokalator's \texttt{/compaction} and \texttt{/preview} commands, which help developers anticipate when their context window will approach the rot threshold and plan conversation strategies accordingly. Notably, VS Code v1.110~\cite{vscode2026v110} subsequently introduced a native \texttt{/compact} command and automatic compaction for Copilot chat sessions, confirming the importance of this capability; Tokalator's approach differs in providing explicit threshold tracking, turn-by-turn growth projection, and cross-provider support rather than session-scoped automation within a single IDE.

\textit{Agent context management:}
Zhang et al.~\cite{zhang2025adaptive} built an adaptive context manager for QA agents that dynamically selects which history fragments to keep based on relevance to the current query --- the same idea Tokalator's tab relevance scorer applies to open IDE files. In code generation, Shi et al.~\cite{shi2024evor} introduced EVOR, which refines retrieved context documents during code synthesis; Tokalator solves the related problem of deciding which already-open files should stay in context. Zhang et al.~\cite{zhang2025ace} introduced Agentic Context Engineering (ACE), which treats the system prompt as a living document that grows richer through generation and reflection, gaining +10.6\% on agent benchmarks while cutting cost. ACE shows that actively managing what enters the context window produces better results than leaving it uncontrolled --- the same principle behind Tokalator's optimization-first design. Nanjundappa and Maaheshwari~\cite{nanjundappa2025branch} proposed ContextBranch, which applies version-control ideas (checkpoint, branch, switch, inject) to LLM conversations, cutting context size by 58.1\% in exploratory coding. ContextBranch and Tokalator target the same problem from different angles: Tokalator controls which files enter the context; ContextBranch controls which conversation turns stay.

\textit{Cross-session and multi-agent context:}
Vasilopoulos~\cite{vasilopoulos2026codified} described Codified Context, a three-part system (hot-memory constitution, 19 specialist agents, cold-memory knowledge base) used across 283 development sessions on a 108,000-line C\# codebase. It is the closest real-world counterpart to Tokalator: Tokalator manages the live context window within a session, while Codified Context organizes persistent cross-session memory to stop LLMs from forgetting project conventions. Together, the two cover the full lifecycle --- within a session (Tokalator) and across sessions (Codified Context). Zhu et al.~\cite{zhu2025onecontext} proposed OneContext, a self-managed context layer for multi-agent systems that records trajectories and supports shared checkpoints; it operates at the multi-agent level, while Tokalator focuses on the single-developer, single-agent context budget inside the IDE.

\textit{Terminology:}
The context engineering field still lacks agreed-on terms. For example, Anthropic calls the feature ``prompt caching,'' OpenAI calls it ``automatic caching,'' and Google calls it ``context caching'' --- three names for mechanically similar features with different pricing rules. Hong et al.~\cite{hong2025contextrot} coined ``context rot,'' while others use ``context degradation,'' ``attention dilution,'' or ``context pollution'' for overlapping ideas. Burnham and Adamczewski~\cite{burnham2025context} introduced ``context engineering'' itself, yet terms like ``compaction,'' ``distractors,'' and ``stable prefix'' remain informal. Tokalator contributes a dictionary of 41 terms across seven categories (context management, token economics, prompt engineering, memory strategies, caching, architecture, and evaluation) at \url{https://tokalator.wiki/dictionary}, and the extension's interface introduces operational terms such as \emph{budget level}, \emph{context health}, \emph{relevance score}, \emph{compaction point}, \emph{rot threshold}, and \emph{optimization score} that link abstract concepts to actionable indicators.

  \item \textit{MCP Server + CLI} (\texttt{tokalator-mcp/}, TypeScript/Node.js ESM): Real Claude BPE token counting for Claude Code via the Model Context Protocol (stdio transport). Exposes four tools: \texttt{count\_tokens}, \texttt{estimate\_budget}, \texttt{preview\_turn}, and \texttt{list\_models}. Also ships a standalone CLI binary (\texttt{tokalator}) installable via npm, with commands \texttt{count}, \texttt{budget}, \texttt{preview}, and \texttt{models}. \end{enumerate}



The web platform's library layer (\texttt{lib/pricing}, \texttt{lib/caching}, \texttt{lib/conversation}, \texttt{lib/context}) provides the computational backend for all seven calculators. The VS~Code extension maintains its own embedded model profiles and tokenizer logic (\texttt{modelProfiles.ts}, \texttt{tokenizerService.ts}) because it runs inside the extension host process and cannot share modules with the web platform. Both sides track the same provider pricing but are maintained independently. Inside the extension, five layers work together: (1)~the \textit{Core Engine} (\texttt{contextMonitor.ts}) reacts to VS~Code editor events and builds \texttt{ContextSnapshot} records; (2)~the \textit{Tokenizer Service} (\texttt{tokenizerService.ts}) counts tokens using provider-specific BPE encoders; (3)~the \textit{Relevance Scorer} (\texttt{tabRelevanceScorer.ts}) assigns each tab a score $R \in [0,1]$; (4)~the \textit{Context Optimizer} closes tabs where $R < 0.3$; and (5)~the \textit{Chat Participant} (\texttt{contextChatParticipant.ts}) exposes 11 slash commands. Full details are given in Section~\ref{sec:functionalities}.

Figure \ref{fig:seq} illustrates the runtime flow. When the developer opens or switches a tab, the Core Engine requests token counts and relevance scores, builds a \texttt{ContextSnapshot}, and pushes it to the Dashboard. When the developer types \texttt{@tokalator /optimize}, the Chat Participant retrieves the current snapshot, scores all open tabs, and closes those below the relevance threshold.

The central data structure is \texttt{ContextSnapshot}, which is emitted on every state change and contains: a timestamp, the active file, a list of all open tabs (each with URI, estimated tokens, relevance score, and diagnostics), the set of pinned files, total estimated tokens, window capacity, usage percentage, budget level (\texttt{low}/\texttt{medium}/\texttt{high}), context health status with reasons, model identifier, workspace-level file statistics, the tokenizer type in use, per-turn history, and a \texttt{BudgetBreakdown} struct that itemizes files, system prompt, instructions, conversation, and output reservation.
